James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Diane Keaton deliver performances that add depth and authenticity to the supporting characters, contributing to the film's overall richness.

Nino Rota's haunting score, featuring the iconic theme that evokes a sense of melancholy and inevitability, serves as the film's emotional backbone. The music complements the narrative's emotional beats, enhancing the audience's connection to the characters' experiences and dilemmas.

In the realm of cinema, "The Godfather" has achieved a legendary status that few films can rival. Its exploration of power dynamics, family loyalty, and the moral grey areas of life resonates across generations. It's a film that rewards multiple viewings, as each revisit uncovers new layers and nuances that contribute to its enduring appeal.

In conclusion, "The Godfather" is a timeless classic that continues to be celebrated for its exceptional performances, masterful storytelling, and impeccable craftsmanship. 10.title: "Leave the gun, take the cannoli."
10.content:
In this Godfather's hyper-violent Waltz it is strictly business, kill, or be killed. The Godfather trilogy directed by Francis Ford Coppola is legendary among movie-critics and fans alike, and capturing generation after generation in the sad, and hungry world of mid-twentieth century organized crime. The casting is excellent with Marlon Brando as the legendary Vito Corleone, the namesake of this film: The Don, the Godfather. Following is Al Pacino's breakout role as Michael Corleone, the youngest of the three Corleone brothers. The story focuses primarily around the Corleone family as a whole, though Michael takes a primary seat as main character as the story progresses further.

The family is very close, as shown in the opening scene at Connie's (Talia Shire) wedding with the big Italian family singing Luna Mezz O' Mare laughing, and having a right old time. Contrast that with Michael who is sitting at a table by himself, almost ashamed of the family he belongs to. He even goes as far as to tell his girlfriend that "It's my family, Kay. It isn't me" when she asks him about the deal that the Don made that couldn't be refused. On the opposite of the quiet Michael is the hotblooded Sunny (James Caan) Corleone, the oldest of the three, smashing cameras of photographers trying to get a picture, and even so much as spitting on the badge of an FBI agent checking license plate numbers

Francis Ford Coppola loves to use close-up scenes meant to inspire uneasiness, or dread followed by wide shots of the characters. A half eaten sandwich is of no real concern to most people, and does not deserve a close-up for the sake of a close-up. However, in the context of a half eaten sandwich at a guard post with no sign of the guard, it leaves an air of curiosity. Where did the guard go, why is he gone? Then another notch further, the guard who isn't there is supposed to be defending the Don who was almost gunned down in the streets only a few scenes prior. Now most viewers I would assume have never had armed hit men after them, but the atmosphere that Coppola has painted up to this scene leaves it clear that the men are coming back, and that the only one who can save the Don is the one person who never wanted to get involved in the business, Michael. This is but one example of many in which ordinary things, or the lack there of, create the atmosphere because death lurks around every corner.

Beside the fantastic screen-play, and the shot compositions, when one remarks upon The Godfather, they should also mention the musical accompaniment which helps build the scenes like no other. The whole soundtrack is primarily written by Nino Rota with minimal exceptions. The one which most everyone knows is the main theme of The Godfather, "The Godfather Waltz" is a very foreboding and slow tune played out on the trumpet for a few moments before being picked up by a few other stringed instruments. Throughout the scenes, the soundtrack might play a more upbeat and serene piece but as soon as you hear that trumpet, all bets are off. It doesn't matter what happened in the scenes prior, somebody is now dancing to The Godfather's tune.

Over-all, The Godfather is a wonderful film I would recommend for anyone to watch along with the entire trilogy. It's the type of film that will last from generation to generation as a truly marvel of a film. That, I can guarantee.

10.title: "The Godfather" - A Timeless Masterpiece
10.content:
"The Godfather," directed by Francis Ford Coppola and released in 1972, stands as a cinematic masterpiece that has not only withstood the test of time but continues to captivate audiences with its compelling storytelling, impeccable acting, and profound exploration of power, family, and the American Dream.

At its core, "The Godfather" is a crime drama that unfolds the saga of the Corleone family, a powerful Italian-American Mafia clan led by the patriarch, Vito Corleone, portrayed flawlessly by Marlon Brando. Brando's performance is iconic, setting a standard for portrayals of organized crime bosses. His nuanced portrayal of Vito, a man torn between his loyalty to family and the brutal realities of his criminal empire, earned him a well-deserved Academy Award.

The film's narrative, based on Mario Puzo's novel of the same name, intricately weaves together themes of power, betrayal, and morality. The screenplay, co-written by Puzo and Coppola, is a triumph in storytelling, presenting a rich tapestry of characters and relationships. The script is laced with memorable quotes, such as "I'm gonna make him an offer he can't refuse," which have become iconic in popular culture.

Beyond its storytelling prowess, "The Godfather" boasts a stellar ensemble cast, featuring performances that have become legendary. Al Pacino's portrayal of Michael Corleone, Vito's reluctant son drawn into the family business, is a revelation. Pacino's transformation from a war hero to a ruthless mob boss is both subtle and powerful, marking the beginning of a career that would solidify him as one of the greatest actors of his generation.

The film's cinematography, courtesy of Gordon Willis, is a visual feast. The use of dark and moody lighting, coupled with long takes and carefully composed shots, adds a layer of gravitas to the narrative. The musical score, composed by Nino Rota, is equally iconic, with its haunting melodies becoming synonymous with the film's atmosphere.

"The Godfather" is more than a crime drama; it's a reflection on the American Dream and the lengths individuals will go to protect their families. The film's impact on cinema is immeasurable, influencing countless directors and setting a standard for the genre. Even decades after its release, "The Godfather" continues to be a cultural touchstone, a testament to its enduring brilliance. If you haven't experienced this cinematic masterpiece, consider it a must-watch that transcends its genre and remains a timeless classic.

Beyond its cinematic achievements, "The Godfather" has become a cultural phenomenon. It has spawned countless references in popular culture, from parodies to homages, further solidifying its status as a touchstone in the collective imagination. Its portrayal of the mafia and its exploration of themes such as loyalty, power, and family have resonated with audiences around the world, transcending language and cultural barriers.

Conclusion:

In the pantheon of cinema, "The Godfather" stands as an unrivaled masterpiece. Its compelling storytelling, iconic performances, visual artistry, and lasting cultural impact have secured its place as one of the greatest films of.

10.title: Family
10.content:
I have a sentimental love for the first Godfather. Though part 2 might itself be a better film, i love the Corleone family because of the first one. Every time i see it, i remember why these people feel like family to me: sonny is like an obnoxious older brother sometimes, hot headed, but genuinely loving and caring. Tom is the level headed man, who takes into consideration the wisest way to handle things and benefit the family. Fredo is the one that everyone loves, just because he can't take care of himself. and Michael, he's everyman isn't he? He has dreams and goals and wants to live his life independent of the influence of his family. but circumstance formulates, and deepens his character. He soon chooses a path that he swore he never would, but he is almost forced to do it. Granted, no one is pointing a gun to his head- but his heart compels him.

and Don Vito himself. An aging king who's love for his family is what keeps him alive even after a brutal assassination attempt. What is he to do about his kingdom? he knows he has little time left, yet, his sons imperfections and his own regrets (though he says he has none) leave him questioning the future. I draw a parallel here to King Lear and even Kurosawa's Ran- Vito Corleone is much like the principal characters in these other two works, though more composed and strong in mind.

Look beyond the violence, the slick talk, the plot. See the love, the family, the relationships. You'll be able to see your own family in the Corleones, as imperfect as they are (being that we need to remember that they are monsters, who murder people for personal gain) and more importantly, you'll be able to see yourself. Not one of us can say that we're any better- we can only say that we've chosen a different road.

10.title: Perfection.
10.content:
"The Godfather" exists within a vacuum: it is without precedent, and (not for the want of much effort), it is without imitation. To try and objectively review this Film, after its effect on my life, would be a poor joke. Frankly, I adore it. It is Romantic, absolutely. Beyond belief. Even Technically, it's a paradise. The colours drip, rich and heavy. The characters hold up a mirror to our psyche, and the dialogue has rightly cemented "The Godfather" as a movie which will always have a relevance. Ironically, this tale of counter-culture has become arguably the definitive Pop Culture statement. "The Godfather" IS the gap between Mainstream and Art. It is the scale to which every "classic" must compare itself, and inevitably fall short. Concise Coalescence: "The Godfather" is the greatest Movie ever made. But that's not why I LOVE it. Sure, I respect a whole bunch of Films. I can recognise a Film's influence, award it its dues, and move on. But I keep coming back to this, because I feel an affection for it. Every time I hear that sweeping Niño Rota score, I'm reminded: this changed my life! Days spent dreaming of my future as either a Mafioso or a Film-maker. To a degree, "The Godfather's" reputation does it a disservice; this isn't a Movie to admire, it's a Movie to FEEL. And I guarantee you, it's so powerful that only a truly emotionally dead person won't feel it.

And so I again ask myself: Why is it I love "The Godfather"? I love "The Godfather" because it never becomes cute or cuddly. I've just waxed lyrical about it, but as I sit to watch it, it's still dark, it's intimidating. It never gives itself up to soppy nostalgia, and that's why it remains as shocking a statement now as it did more than a quarter of a century ago. Perfection.

Epic in scope while maintaining a patience and intimacy characteristic of European art cinema, THE GODFATHER is rightly considered one of the greatest films ever made. The Godfather continues to influence producers of films, television shows, and video games more than 30 years after its release. Nino Rota's score, the sumptuous set design, and Brando's raspy pseudo-whisper have become part of our collective cultural memory.

The film possesses an operatic quality, yet it's more understated than it is flamboyant. It takes its subjects seriously, bestowing legitimacy upon the internecine power struggles of the Mafia normally reserved for classical themes in high art. The film's release initiated a period when American filmmakers dared to take themselves and their artistic ambitions seriously (perhaps too seriously). There is something deeply resonant in the film's treatment of filial piety, the need for respect, and our culture's abiding interest in the parallel moral universe of the Mafia.

10.title: incredile
10.content: I was roughly twenty years away from even being conceived when The Godfather came out. Growing up as a film nut, I often heard of The Godfather as possessing a sort of mythic status that few films made after 1955 possess. I first watched it back close to ten years ago as a 12-year-old, never fully getting the story with the film falling into the "great film that I didn't appreciate" category until a month or so back when I got the Coppola restoration Blu-Ray and realized as an adult how fantastic of a film it truly was. The Godfather works so well because it isn't a film that kisses its ass on a variety of sub-levels. Francis Ford Coppola went out of his way not to make the film one that glorifies the Mafia in any way but still realized what a magnificent project it was. It begins in celebration and ends as the first part of the trilogy in bitter-sweet victory and tragedy for the Corleones with Michael having slowly morphed into a different character by the end and the Corleone family itself has endured tragedy after tragedy. Depending on if you're selective to certain genres of movies -- particularly crime and heist thrillers -- the 1970s were either a fantastic time with the New Hollywood group of directors or a pitiful time where the Anti-Hero was all the rage. I've always tried to keep a foot in both camps for the most part, but if a film like this doesn't make you at least sit there as the credits roll, musing in thought like Indiana Jones after being given a clue by a recently-killed shaman or anti-Nazi spy the first time you watch it, then I'm not sure you know how to appreciate films and movies as art and not just entertainment. There are so many ways this film just works so well; the first is that Coppola always had a way of making the cinematography and direction style look both extravagant, but also bleak at the same time, partially through sun-faded cinematography (I'm just guessing) and also partially through the way the film itself was shot. As well fact that Coppola spared nothing when it came to deploying talented screen stars of the day to cast The Godfather, leading Marlon Brando to find international success once more with his portrayal of Vito Corleone, Al Pacino as the reluctant, but the eventual successor to his father Vito, Michael Corleone, Diane Keaton as Kay Adams, Robert Duvall as Tom Hagen, and of course, a pre-Rocky Talia Shire as Connie Corleone. These cast members in particular stand out in their performances and convey a sort of detached emotion that makes the film so great (if you need clarification on this, the scene where Vito overlooks his own son's body in the morgue is a prime example). Although it is the best install installment Godfather trilogy, the film itself suffers from a few key points that I've never been able to reason out why were included. Specifically, the whole sequence involves Johnny Fontaine and the Woltz horse fiasco which has no real involvement in the over-arcing storyline. However, with how spectacular of a film it is, I'm not going to sit here and complain about it any further.

The Godfather (1972): Review

Nearly five decades since its release, Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather" remains a towering achievement in cinema, captivating new generations with its timeless storytelling and compelling characters. Adapted from Mario Puzo's bestselling novel, this seminal film not only redefined the gangster genre but also solidified its place in the pantheon of cinematic classics.

Plot and Themes

"The Godfather" intricately weaves the saga of the Corleone family, a powerful Mafia dynasty in post-World War II America. At its core, it's a story about power, loyalty, and the complex dynamics of family. The film's narrative arc, focusing on the transformation of Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) from a reluctant outsider to a ruthless Mafia boss, serves as a poignant exploration of the corrupting influence of power and the inevitable moral decay it brings.

Direction and Cinematography

Coppola's direction is masterful, balancing grandiose set pieces with intimate character moments. His use of lighting, particularly the chiaroscuro technique, creates a moody and atmospheric visual style that enhances the film's dark, brooding tone. Gordon Willis, the cinematographer, earned the nickname "The Prince of Darkness" for his innovative use of shadows and low-light scenes, which remain visually stunning even by today's standards.

Performances

The film boasts a stellar cast, with Marlon Brando delivering an iconic performance as Vito Corleone. His portrayal is both powerful and nuanced, conveying the duality of a ruthless crime lord and a loving family patriarch. Al Pacino's subtle, evolving performance as Michael Corleone is equally compelling, marking his emergence as one of the finest actors of his generation. The supporting cast, including James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Diane Keaton, each bring depth and authenticity to their roles, enriching the film's complex tapestry.

Cultural Impact and Legacy

"The Godfather" has left an indelible mark on popular culture. Its influence extends beyond cinema into television, literature, and even video games. Iconic lines like "I'll make him an offer he can't refuse" have permeated everyday language. The film's depiction of the Mafia has been both criticized and celebrated for its romanticized yet brutally honest portrayal of organized crime.

Modern Relevance

Revisiting "The Godfather" today, its themes of power, corruption, and family loyalty are as relevant as ever. The film's exploration of the American Dream, juxtaposed with the immigrant experience and the pursuit of success at any cost, resonates strongly in contemporary discussions about identity and morality in modern society.

Conclusion

In a modern context, "The Godfather" stands as a paragon of cinematic excellence. Its rich storytelling, unforgettable performances, and profound themes ensure that it remains not only a cornerstone of film history but also a pertinent and compelling narrative for today's audience. Whether you are a first-time viewer or revisiting the film, "The Godfather" offers a profound and unforgettable experience, affirming its status as a masterpiece that transcends time.

10.title: A Cinematic Masterpiece: The Godfather
10.content:
The Godfather, directed by Francis Ford Coppola, stands as a timeless masterpiece that has captured the hearts and minds of audiences for decades. This epic crime drama, based on Mario Puzo's novel of the same name, delves deep into the intricate world of the Italian-American mafia, delivering a captivating narrative, brilliant performances, and unparalleled filmmaking.

The film's narrative follows the Corleone family, led by the enigmatic Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) and his reluctant son, Michael (Al Pacino). Set against the backdrop of post-World War II America, The Godfather weaves a complex tale of power, family loyalty, honor, and the devastating consequences of violence. The script is flawlessly written, expertly blending intense drama, suspense, and moments of unexpected tenderness.

One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its exceptional cast. Marlon Brando's portrayal of Don Vito Corleone is legendary, capturing the essence of a powerful and respected mafia leader with a remarkable balance of strength and vulnerability. Al Pacino delivers a career-defining performance as Michael Corleone, subtly transforming from a reluctant outsider to a calculating and ruthless heir apparent. The supporting cast, including James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Diane Keaton, also shine in their respective roles, adding depth and complexity to the story.

Beyond the performances, The Godfather is a visual and auditory marvel. Coppola's meticulous attention to detail brings 1940s New York to life, immersing the audience in a meticulously recreated world. The film's cinematography, complemented by a hauntingly beautiful score by Nino Rota, adds to the overall ambiance, creating an atmosphere that is both captivating and atmospheric.

The Godfather's enduring legacy can be attributed to its exploration of universal themes that transcend its criminal underworld setting. Themes of power, family, loyalty, and the consequences of choices resonate with audiences on a profound level. The film's narrative complexity and its examination of moral ambiguity continue to provoke thought and discussion, even decades after its release.

While The Godfather is undeniably a lengthy film, every minute is filled with purpose and significance. The pacing is deliberate, allowing the story to unfold organically and drawing viewers deeper into its intricate web. Each scene is carefully crafted, leaving an indelible impression and contributing to the film's overall impact.

In conclusion, The Godfather is a cinematic tour de force that sets the standard for storytelling, character development, and filmmaking excellence. Its profound exploration of themes, stellar performances, meticulous craftsmanship, and unforgettable moments make it a true masterpiece. Whether you're a fan of crime dramas or simply appreciate exceptional filmmaking, The Godfather is an absolute must-see that continues to captivate and enthrall audiences to this day.

10.title: Wonderful film
10.content: The Godfather is a technically instructive film with its dark and realistic atmosphere. The cinematographer of the movie, Gordon Willis, used shadows and contrast in such a way that you say this is the movie while watching it. While watching the dark and beautiful atmosphere, you also watch the plot. Some people may be bored in the first scenes while watching the movie, but I was not bored because the mafia theme was a theme that I loved before. The film chronicles the conflict between the Carlone family and Comma Solozzo over her drug business. Don Carleone politely declines the offer, calling it a "dope" dirty job, but Solozzo, who is not very happy about it, arranges an assassination on Carleone himself, causing things to heat up. This is the crux of the movie. We are watching the characteristic change of Michael, who normally has little to do with family affairs. Michel first kills Solozzo to avenge his father's death, and then takes over the family business. It's as if that innocent child who watches family affairs from afar is gone, replaced by a calm but cold killer. Michael is actually the opposite of his brother Sonny. While Sonny is an irrational person who cannot control his anger, Micheal is logical and just as calm. Although "The Godfather" is a crime movie, it is actually a movie based on the father and son relationship. The best example for this is the scene where Don Vito and Michael are alone. In this scene, Carleone says that she has always worked for her family all her life, and that she will not be ashamed to work, but that she has never thought of Michael as the head of the family. It was a pretty good movie for me, but I can understand that it might not appeal to everyone. In this movie, your main focus is not on the life of the mafia, but on the fact that you cannot trust anyone but your family and you have no one but them. Otherwise, why would anyone turn their family into a criminal organization? We see in the movie that almost everyone betrayed the father except his sons. (Virgül Solozzo, Tattaglia family, Carlo, Tessio) When I said you can't trust anyone but your family, I meant this. Finally, I have a cut-off message that I don't like the Godfather and hate him all his life: Watch The Godfather not as a mafia movie, but as a father and son movie because only then can you love this movie. Enjoy or hate the mafia theme.

10.title: A Grand Masterpiece....
10.content:
Almost every person who sees Hollywood films has at least heard of The Godfather, it is considered by multiple sources as one of the best films ever made in history, many people have also claimed that this is the best film ever made. I am not sure if I agree with the latter point, but I can proudly say is that the Godfather is just a Grand masterpiece which not only a fan of the crime genre but anyone who likes movies in general can enjoy.

Now this is a 1972 film some people say it has not aged well, I disagree that film is still entertaining to watch, the plot will still grasp your attention and you will still be on the edge of your seat. The main thing that this movie does different compared to the movies of today's generation that it moves at a very very slow pace not that it's a bad thing, back then almost all films did that, the minor scenes went on for quite long. I mean seriously has there even been a recent movie in which a party or wedding scene went on for over 10 minutes (unless the actual film was based upon it)?

Now I will not take away from this movie because of of prolonged scenes because the movie still makes sure to progress its story slowly in such scenes to keep the viewer interested. However these scenes also make the movie go on for 3 hours which kind of hurts its replay value. But even if you watch the Godfather once you will simply be in awe of it's magnificent story, brilliant characters and perfect setting and environment.

This film is also a very realistic portrayal of mobs in Italy during that time period. All actors bring the characters to life and very so into the characters that you will feel like they are the characters themselves rather than actual actors. The acting is simply among the best I have seen in any movie, not just from the lead Al Pacino and Marlon Brando but even the supporting characters like Sonny played by James Caan or Tom Hagen, played by Robert Duvall are fantastically portrayed. Even the minor and the female characters play their part to perfection. There is nothing really bad to say about the acting.

The plot is about the Corleone family and how it tries to co-exist with the other mobs. The story is fantastic with many twists and turns throughout and will keep you engaged about what will happen next, the movie does not move rapidly fast but it moves at a very slow pace to allow the viewer to get a better idea of the characters and the plot. The ending is also fantastic and is a perfect example of character development.

The soundtrack is also fantastic and fits all the scenes in the movie, the main theme of the film in particular still sounds awesome even to this very day. The movie also takes itself very seriously, it does not do comedy, apart from a very few and rare scenes, this film is very serious and rightfully so it deals with a very serious topic and the events that transpire throughout are very difficult, tragic and severe for this movie to be anything else. The film is violent but it is not what you see throughout 90% of the film, the violence which is there, serves its purpose and progresses the plot in a meaningful way.

Apart from the pacing, I felt like this film was a little hard to understand sometimes without subtitles specially when the Italian language is spoken, we are still not completely clueless to what's actually going on but knowing what the characters are actually saying would have helped. But that is only a minor issue which does not take away from the overall film.

In the end, I just want to say what has already been said many times, The Godfather one of the best films ever made in history and anyone who likes Hollywood cinema in general and still hasn't watched this masterpiece, should just watch this classic, this is Hollywood at it's very finest.

Overall Rating: 10/10

The Godfather is considered by most to be one of the finest films ever made, with good reason. It's unforgettable.

It's beautiful. The cinematography is legendary, from the dark hallways of the family home in New York to the bright, sunny skies of Sicily, this movie is a feast for the eyes. And the soundtrack, mostly written by Nino Rota, perfectly accompanies the visuals to complete the atmosphere.

It's an acting clinic. There has arguably never been a better cast for a movie. No fewer than four actors - Brando, Pacino, Caan and Duvall - received acting nominations. It's likely that having three characters nominated for best supporting actor cost Pacino the much deserved Oscar (which went to Joel Gray for Cabaret). Al Pacino has gone on to a celebrated, illustrious career, but he was never better than he was here. But James Caan as Santino and Robert Duvall as Tom Hagen were also terrific. And then there was Marlon Brando's performance, which dominates the screen whenever he's on.

It's a study in dichotomy. These characters were mobsters, stone cold killers who chilled to the bone. And yet they were devoted to their family and absolutely loyal.

It's also a study in character development. We see Michael begin as a man of principle and character who rejects the family business, but at a time of need he joins his family to defend his father's life. From that point we watch him descend, little by little, until at the end he's a monster himself. No other movie shows so artfully a man lose his soul.

And apart from all that, it's quite entertaining. I can recommend no other movie more highly.

10.title: Precisely why I feel this is the greatest movie of all time

I honestly think this is the finest piece of cinema I have every viewed (but then again, I can't claim to have seen vast quantities of movies). Firstly, the aesthetics mark it out as a classic: some shots, such as those of Vito Corleone in his study, could be removed from the film and considered art by themselves. Not only are the costumes beautiful, the lighting, sets and movement makes the film absolutely stunning, visually. All scenes appear to have a mild sepia tint and the lights particularly focus our eyes on peoples' expressions.

Of course a film cannot survive on aesthetic beauty alone: the subtlety in the acting is superb. Al Pacino's face fleshes out his character perfectly and the mannerisms and prescence of each character is distinct and revealing. Although it is occasionally difficult to understand Marlon Brando, his screen prescence is astonishing and he, as the head of the family, he dominates his scenes. Yet there is something in Michael Corleone that singles him out, and Al Pacino really brings this to the role.

I am less interested in the film's social commentary, although it is present and strong. The film has a distinctly 'epic' feel to it and as a result seems relatively objective. It does an astonishing job of presenting the characters as human beings and brothers and fathers and friends. In most films, the same characters would be painted by the film as either violent thugs or murderers. Of course, the director does not insult our intelligence, and this is what makes the film so good: Michael Corleone is a murderer and a thug, and the film does not hide this; yet we identify with him and we understand his motives and his mind. By the end of the film he is cold-blooded, a killer and has his brother-in-law murdered. Yet we look at him as a member of a family, not as a Mafia Don. He is one of the finest characters in movie history.

10.title: A Masterpiece and film history
10.content:
The remarkable thing about Mario Puzo's novel was the way it seemed to be told from the inside out; he didn't give us a world of international intrigue, but a private club as constricted as the seventh grade. Everybody knew everybody else and had a pretty shrewd hunch what they were up to. The movie (based on a script labored over for some time by Puzo and then finally given form, I suspect, by director Francis Ford Coppola) gets the same feel. We tend to identify with Don Corleone's family not because we dig gang wars, but because we have been with them from the beginning, watching them wait for battle while sitting at the kitchen table and eating chow mein out of paper cartons. "The Godfather" himself is not even the central character in the drama. That position goes to the youngest, brightest son, Michael, who understands the nature of his father's position while revising his old-fashioned ways. The Godfather's role in the family enterprise is described by his name; he stands outside the next generation which will carry on and, hopefully, angle the family into legitimate enterprises. Those who have read the novel may be surprised to find Michael at the center of the movie, instead of Don Corleone. In fact, this is simply an economical way for Coppola to get at the heart of the Puzo story, which dealt with the transfer of power within the family. Marlon Brando, who plays the Godfather as a shrewd, unbreakable old man, actually has the character lead in the movie; Al Pacino, with a brilliantly developed performance as Michael, is the lead. Although the movie is three hours long, it absorbs us so effectively it never has to hurry. There is something in the measured passage of time as Don Corleone hands over his reins of power that would have made a shorter, faster moving film unseemly. Even at this length, there are characters in relationships you can't quite understand unless you've read the novel. Or perhaps you can, just by the way the characters look at each other.

Coppola has found a style and a visual look for all this material so "The Godfather" becomes something of a rarity: a really good movie squeezed from a bestseller. The decision to shoot everything in period decor (the middle and late 1940s) was crucial; if they'd tried to save money as they originally planned, by bringing everything up-to-date, the movie simply wouldn't have worked.

10.title: The Godfather (1972, Francis Ford Coppola) The quintessential American film
10.content:
'The Godfather' is a classic American film from 1972 directed by Francis Ford Coppola based on the novel by Mario Puzo. The film has gone down in cinematic history, and is lauded as one of the greatest American films ever made. Not only was it the highest grossing film of 1972, but it went on to win three Academy Awards including Best Picture, Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Actor for Marlon Brando who famously declined the award. Along with Brando the film stars numerous actors who went on to become household names such as Al Pacino, Diane Keaton, Robert Duvall and James Caan among others.

The film focuses on the Corleone family who are one of the major mafia families operating in New York City at the time and only one generation removed from their immigration to America from Sicily. While Vito, played by Brando, is the head of the family the film focuses on his youngest son Michael's rise to power after Vito is shot and later passes away. Michael, played by Pacino, understands and appreciates the family business, but starts on the outside as a more straight laced, by the book member of the family rather than the rest of his mafia entrenched siblings. It becomes clear as the story progresses, though, that Michael must transform and take the reins and usher the family into the future, and in doing so he must shed all of his nicety and embrace a more pragmatic and brutal method.

There is almost nothing you can say about the 'The Godfather' that is not a superlative from the production itself such as directing, cinematography and music to the story which is broad, sweeping and empathetic yet also intimate and heartfelt. At the time all people thought of gangsters and the mafia were the exploitation films of Edward G. Robinson and James Cagney. There hadn't been a serious movie about these people to that point. The actors in 'The Godfather' are all operating on another level. It is clear why Brando was so key to cast in the film as it is unimaginable, at this point, to think of anyone else as Vito Corleone, and the film took an unknown, soft spoken Pacino and made him a star. Puzo and Coppola's script is brilliant smashing the idea that an author could not adapt their own work. If there is one criticism I have with the story it is how Michael deals with Kay. She was Michael's girlfriend and when Michael must flee the country after he commits a double homicide she is just cut out of his life. Michael woos a local girl in Sicily, marries her and becomes a widow before returning to America. Once back he waits a year to approach Kay and reestablish a romantic connection. I felt that whole storyline was problematic and in poor taste, but in the grand scheme of the story and production it is really a small complaint. This film is universally praised and deservedly so. It has stood the test of time and has cemented itself for all time as one of the greatest American films of all time.

Eric's Grade: A.

10.title: Unbelievable
10.content:
**"The Godfather" (1972) - A Monumental Epic of Power and Family**

Francis Ford Coppola's *The Godfather*, released in 1972, is widely regarded as one of the greatest films in cinema history. Adapted from Mario Puzo's best-selling novel, this epic gangster saga is a masterclass in storytelling, direction, and performance, and it has left an indelible mark on film and popular culture.

Set against the backdrop of post-World War II America, *The Godfather* chronicles the life and evolution of the Corleone crime family, led by patriarch Vito Corleone, played with gravitas and nuance by Marlon Brando. The film opens with the Corleone family's patriarch, Don Vito Corleone, overseeing his empire with a blend of paternal affection and ruthless efficiency. The story is as much about the Corleones' criminal enterprise as it is about the family dynamics and the inevitable shift of power that comes with the changing times.

At its core, *The Godfather* is a profound exploration of family loyalty, power, and the cost of ambition. The narrative follows Michael Corleone (Al Pacino), the youngest son of Vito Corleone, who initially distances himself from the family business. Michael's journey from reluctant outsider to ruthless crime boss is central to the film's dramatic arc and reflects a larger commentary on the corrupting influence of power. Pacino's portrayal of Michael is nothing short of extraordinary, capturing the character's complex evolution with subtlety and intensity.

The screenplay, co-written by Coppola and Puzo, is a tightly woven tapestry of intrigue and betrayal. It deftly balances multiple storylines and richly developed characters, creating a world where personal and political motivations intertwine. The dialogue is crisp and laden with dramatic weight, contributing to the film's immersive atmosphere. Lines like "I'm gonna make him an offer he can't refuse" have become iconic, encapsulating the film's thematic essence and its exploration of the consequences of loyalty and power.

Visually, *The Godfather* is a cinematic marvel. Gordon Willis' cinematography, often referred to as the "Prince of Darkness" for his use of shadow and low lighting, creates a mood of ominous foreboding that enhances the film's dramatic tension. The lighting and composition underscore the film's themes, with shadowy scenes reflecting the moral ambiguity of the characters and the dark underbelly of their world.

The film's score, composed by Nino Rota, is another standout element. The hauntingly beautiful theme music not only enhances the film's emotional resonance but also helps to establish its distinctive atmosphere. The score's blend of Italian folk influences and classical elements underscores the film's exploration of heritage and tradition.

The supporting cast is equally stellar. James Caan delivers a fiery performance as Sonny Corleone, the hot-headed eldest son, while Robert Duvall's portrayal of Tom Hagen, the Corleone family's consigliere, adds depth and nuance to the narrative. Each character is meticulously crafted, contributing to the film's rich tapestry of family and crime.

Coppola's direction is a testament to his vision and skill. He manages to blend epic storytelling with intimate character studies, creating a film that is both grand in scale and deeply personal. His meticulous attention to detail and ability to draw out nuanced performances from his actors are key to the film's success and enduring legacy.

The climax of *The Godfather* is a powerful testament to the film's themes. The final scenes, particularly the juxtaposition of Michael's baptism with the brutal elimination of his enemies, underscore the complex interplay between personal and criminal justice. This moment crystallizes Michael's transformation and the ultimate cost of his ascent to power.

In conclusion, *The Godfather* is a cinematic masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences with its powerful storytelling, complex characters, and profound themes. Its exploration of family, power, and morality, combined with exceptional performances and direction, makes it a timeless classic. Its influence on the gangster genre and its impact on film as a whole underscore its place as one of the greatest achievements in cinema history.

10.title: The Godfather": A Cinematic Triumph Amidst Logistical Challenges
10.content:
"The Godfather," directed by Francis Ford Coppola, stands as a timeless masterpiece in the world of cinema, captivating audiences with its powerful storytelling, memorable performances, and intricate portrayal of the Italian-American Mafia. Behind the scenes, however, lay a web of logistical challenges that, remarkably, did not hinder the film's rise to cinematic greatness.

Set in the gritty underworld of New York City, "The Godfather" demanded authenticity in its depiction of the Corleone crime family. This meant finding suitable filming locations that not only matched the vision of 1940s New York but also provided the necessary atmosphere for the film's narrative depth. Coppola and his team scouted extensively, ultimately choosing various sites across New York City and its boroughs.

One of the most iconic locations in the film is the Corleone family estate, a symbol of power and tradition. This estate, filmed at 110 Longfellow Avenue in Staten Island, required meticulous attention to detail. From the grand interiors to the sprawling gardens, each scene demanded precise set design and logistics to transport viewers to the heart of the Corleone dynasty.

However, the challenges extended beyond mere set design. "The Godfather" boasted an ensemble cast of extraordinary talent, including Marlon Brando, Al Pacino, and James Caan. Coordinating the schedules of these acclaimed actors was no small feat, especially considering the depth of their character development throughout the film's narrative arc.

Furthermore, the film's sprawling storyline, adapted from Mario Puzo's novel of the same name, required careful orchestration of filming sequences. From the intimate family moments to the explosive crescendos of violence, each scene had to be meticulously planned and executed.

Perhaps one of the most notable logistical feats was the creation of Little Italy, a key setting in the film. Recreating this vibrant neighborhood in the early 1940s required transforming a section of East Harlem into a bustling, authentic Italian enclave. From period-accurate storefronts to the lively street scenes, the production team spared no effort in immersing viewers in the world of the Corleones.

Adding to the complexity was the need for realism in the film's action sequences. The Godfather's iconic horse head scene, for instance, required delicate handling to create a chillingly believable moment that would resonate with audiences for generations.

Despite these challenges, Francis Ford Coppola's meticulous attention to detail and unwavering vision propelled "The Godfather" to become one of the most revered films in cinematic history. The film's authenticity, gripping performances, and rich storytelling have cemented its status as a timeless classic.

In the end, the logistical hurdles faced during the filming of "The Godfather" only serve to enhance its legend. Each challenge was met with creative solutions and unwavering dedication, resulting in a film that continues to captivate and enthrall audiences, decade after decade.

"The Godfather" stands as a testament to the power of cinema, where even the most daunting logistical challenges can be overcome in service of creating a true work of art.

This review of "The Godfather" barely scratches the surface of its brilliance, but hopefully, it offers a glimpse into the monumental effort that went into bringing this cinematic masterpiece to life.

10.title: GodFather
10.content: This movie change my life.To make a true epic, you need all of three following ingredients working in near perfect harmony. For screenwriters who come across this, take the following pointers on board: 1) Contrasting Characters: Good films have some character distinction, but most fall rather flat because the core of each character is the same.Of course, there are exceptions to rule (ie... where you want mono-tonal characters... aka matrix; or where you want outlandish contrasts... aka The Fifth Element), but ultimately, this is what makes films deep, meaningful and grand. Consider the contrasts between the Don's children. Michael is rather cool, rational and collected, whereas Sonny is more hot-headed, spontaneous and simple minded. But simply having these contrasts is not nearly enough. What you really need to do is to develop these characters - place them in situations - and then dwell on how their character impacts on the situation they're put in. The Godfather is a terrific example of how to pull this off. While many try to do this in screenplays, most lose the plot and create character obscurities that stretch credibility.

10.title: I'm going to make him an offer he can't refuse.
10.content:
I finally finished watching The Godfather (1972) for the first time ever and I absolutely loved it. This movie is officially in my top 10 favorite movies of all time.

Positives for The Godfather (1972): This movie literally has everything that I love about cinema and it is absolutely glorious. Everything from the direction, screenplay, writing, story, editing, pacing, sound design, score, production value, set design, costumes, cinematography and acting are all perfect from the very beginning to the end credits. Theacting from the entire cast is phenomenal and every character in this movie was perfectly casted. Vito Corleone is one of the greatest movie characters in cinematic history and Marlon Brando gives one of the greatest acting performance in all of cinema. I also loved Al Pacino as Michael Corleone, James Caan as Sonny Corleone, Richard Castellano as Peter Clemenza, Robert Duvall as Tom Hagen, Diane Keaton as Kay Adams-Corleone and Abe Vigoda as Salvatore Tessio. I could honestly talk about everyone else in this movie, but I would say the same thing over and over again because they are all that damn good in this movie. The movie is almost 3-hours of characters having conversations in different settings throughout the runtime and for some people that could be very boring, but in here it is all done masterfully by director Francis Ford Coppola. I was so invested and engaged with all of these conversations during my viewing experience because again everyone is perfectly casted in this movie and the dialogue is some of the best I've heard in any movie that I've watched in my entire life. This movie also manages to be perfectly paced with its almost 3-hour runtime. The shootouts, violence and kill sprees in this movie are all staged perfectly and while it may seem tamed compared to modern day movies like the John Wick Franchise or literally any horror movie in existence, Francis Ford Coppola did a spectacular job at making these scenes very effective. And finally as someone who watched The Offer (2022) online back in 2022, it is truly amazing how this movie ended being as good as it is especially given all of the drama that went on during the development and production of this movie.

Overall, The Godfather (1972) has both earned and deserves its legendary status as a landmark in cinema over 50 years later. For anyone who hasn't watched this movie yet, you need to do so as soon as possible because this is one of those movies that needs to be watched by everyone. The Godfather (1972) is one of the greatest movies in cinematic history and it is one of my favorite movies of all time.

10.title: **** (Out of four)
10.content:
"The Godfather" is one of the crossroads one must cross before proclaiming oneself a movie fan and a genuine movie buff. Francis Ford Coppola's film is probably his most flawless, although it is NOT my favorite Coppola film (that honor belongs to the unmistakably problematic but highly visionary "Apocalypse Now"). Still, in the midst of a 90s cinema which seems to re-evalutate itself every five years or so with new computer-generated images and thusly cannot enjoy the same degree of timelessness of several earlier, better movies, "The Godfather" will undoubtedly hold its own as one of the most artistic endeavors in the relatively new medium of cinema.

The story has been told many times before: based on Mario Puzo's bestseller, the film examines the aura of the Italian Mafiosi as exemplified through the Corleone family, led by patriarch Vito (Marlon Brando, an Oscar winner in a very professional bit of acting). WWII-hero Michael (Al Pacino--the real star of the film as well as the real Best Actor of that year) comes home and breaks family tradition at his sister Connie's wedding ceremony not only by wearing his military uniform, but introducing his family to his WASP-ish girlfriend Kay Adams (Diane Keaton), the epitome of modernistic feminine and Protestant intentions in the Corleone's traditional Catholic--and increasingly outdated--worldview. The wedding scene is one of the great expositions of cinema, and yet the film lives up to all expectations by dashing us headlong into the Corleone's violent world. Of course who can forget the severed horse head in the mansion of the luxurious Hollywood producer, the murder of Luca Brasi, "sleeping with the fishes", Santino's bloody murder at the toll booth, Brando's death scene, the intercutting between the baptism and the murders, and especially the final scene as the door closes and Kay realizes the deceit her entire life will become? To launch into a detailed discussion of Coppola's masterly filmmaking would take beyond 1000 words, so let me just echo the comments of many when saying "The Godfather" is that priceless canoli one should always cherish amidst the decaying corpses of escalating Hollywood trash.

It's an enriching, engrossing, and evocative look into the criminal underworld in perspective of the Corleone family. This is also one of the rarest films to come out without any flaws. As far as it goes, The Godfather is literature for movie-goers and respectfulness for critics. It boasts legendary performances, excellent direction, a brilliant script, and a smooth, peaceful soundtrack.

10.title: Nothing Compares
10.content: A 1972 thriller encapsulating the slow destruction of a valuable family. The crime film, based on Mario Puzo's best selling 1969 novel of the same name - saw Puzo also co-write the screenplay alongside Coppola. Despite many debates over casting, Marlon Brando and Al Pacino portrayed their roles with excellence, not to mention James Caan and the evergreen Diane Keaton. A big hit in its day, the movie was the highest grossing in 1972, between $246 and $287, worth the $80,000 paramount paid to have license to Puzo's book. Spanning from 1945 to 1955, the film endures suffering, passion, tension and love, exploring the ruthless and dark profession in the mafia. In 1945 New York City, at his daughter Connie's wedding to Carlo, Vito Corleone listens to requests in his role as don of the Corleone crime family. His youngest son, Michael, who was a Marine during World War II introduces his girlfriend, Kay Adams, to his family at the reception. Johnny Fontane, a popular singer and Vito's godson, seeks Vito's help in securing a movie role; Vito dispatches his consigliere, Tom Hagen, to Los Angeles to persuade studio head Jack Woltz to give Johnny the part. Woltz refuses until he wakes up in bed with the severed head of his prized stallion, showing that the Corleone's mean business. Brando's character is presented as conservative, worshipped and extremely authoritative, his work is his priority and his peculiar yet sinister speech reinforces his power. Shortly before Christmas, drug baron Sollozo backed by the Tattaglia crime family, asks Vito for investment in his narcotics business and protection through his political connections. Wary of involvement in a dangerous new trade that risks alienating political insiders, Vito declines. Suspicious, Vito sends his enforcer, Luca Brasi, to spy on them. Brasi is garrotted to death during his first meeting with Bruno Tattaglia and Sollozzo. Later, Sollozzo kidnaps Hagen, then has Vito gunned down in the street. With Corleone's first-born Sonny in command, Sollozzo pressures Hagen to persuade Sonny to accept Sollozzo's deal, then releases him. The family receives fish wrapped in Brasi's bullet-proof vest, indicating that Luca "sleeps with the fishes". Vito survives, and at the hospital, Michael thwarts another attempt on his father. Michael's jaw is broken by NYPD Capt. McCluskey, Sollozzo's unofficial bodyguard. Sonny retaliates with a hit on Tattaglia. Michael plots to murder Sollozzo and McCluskey; feigning a desire to settle the dispute, Michael meets them in a Bronx restaurant, where after retrieving a handgun planted by Clemenza, a Corleone capo, he kills both men. Michael (Al Pacino) having just returned from the war, initially wants little or no involvement in the Corleone's business, yet is almost manipulated into performing such a consequential crime. His characterisation is relaxed and the individual is often happy to take a back seat, but, as he is embroiled further in the family business, he creates unprecedented distance between himself and Kay. Despite a clampdown by the authorities, the Five Families erupt in open warfare, and Vito fears for his sons' safety. Michael takes refuge in Sicily and Fredo is sheltered by Moe Greene in Las Vegas. Sonny attacks Carlo on the street for abusing Connie and threatens to kill him if it happens again. When it does, Sonny speeds to their home but is ambushed at a highway toll booth and violently murdered by gangsters wielding submachine guns. While in Sicily, Michael meets and marries Apollonia, but a car bomb intended for him takes her life. We as viewers slowly see the descending reputation of the Corleone family - with Michael forced to keep a low profile, many attempted murders on Vito and the brutal death of Sonny. Devastated by Sonny's death and realising that the Tattaglias are controlled by the now-dominant don, Barzini, Vito attempts to end the feud. He assures the Five Families that he will withdraw his opposition to their heroin business and forgo avenging Sonny's murder. His safety guaranteed, Michael returns home to enter the family business and marry Kay, promising her that the business will be legitimate within five years. Kay gives birth to two children by the early 1950s. With his father nearing the end of his life and Fredo too weak, Michael takes the family reins. He insists Hagen relocate to Las Vegas and relinquish his role to Vito because Hagen is not a "wartime consigliere"; Vito agrees Hagen should "have no part in what will happen" in the coming battles with the rival families. When Michael travels to Las Vegas to buy out Greene's stake in the family's casinos, he is dismayed to see that Fredo is more loyal to Greene than to his own family. We see a transition in Michael's overall attitude, far more assertive and much less reluctant. His loyalties are now firm with the Corleone family, contrasting to his commitments returning from his work as a marine. The protagonist shows no signs of grief following the death of his short-term lover Apollonia, seeing it instead as an excuse to leave Sicily and take full control back in New York. In 1955, Vito suffers a fatal heart attack. At the funeral, Tessio, a Corleone capo, asks Michael to meet with Barzini, signalling the betrayal that Vito had forewarned. The meeting is set for the same day as the baptism of Connie's baby. While Michael stands at the altar as the child's godfather, Corleone hitmen murder the other New York City dons and Greene. Tessio's treachery leads to his execution. Michael extracts Carlo's confession to his complicity in setting up Sonny's murder for Barzini; Clemenza garrottes Carlo to death. Connie accuses Michael of the murder, telling Kay that Michael ordered all the killings. Kay is relieved when Michael finally denies it, but when the capos arrive, they address her husband as Don Corleone and she watches them pay reverence to Michael as the newly installed don as they close the door on her. In all its beauty, we are privileged to visualise such a spectacle. As one 'Godfather' falls, another rises. Once Michael was in the business, he couldn't bring himself to leave, Al Pacino convincingly creates the innocence of the character from the outside, contrasting to his cunning nature inside. The cinematography is well-ahead of its times, most notably in the wedding scene. In the peculiar cyclical structure, the film began at Connie and Carlo's wedding with Vito as the head don. Since then the family quite literally crumbled; Carlo's abuse towards Connie fuelled anger inside of Sonny, who was brutally murdered on his way to protect her. Fredo Corleone preferred life away from the family, Michael initially disregarded the occupation, but, he was tempted by the power and authority that accommodates. His role as 'head' in the family saw his relationship with Kay deteriorate, something that he wasn't aware he was doing. Grabbing a well-deserved Academy Award for Best Actor. Possessing an ultimate calmness and collectedness, Brando portrays Vito's commanding jurisdictions and intimidation's. Most impressively, the American actor perfects the distinctive, soft-spoken tone of voice, reinforcing the brilliance of 'The Godfather'.

10.title: Tragedy and Craft
10.content:
This is one of those titans of cinema. A film so large and firmly ensconced in the collective consciousness of the film world that one does not speak against it and get taken very seriously. Well, I'm not going to speak against that consensus. Not because I cannot think for myself, but because I see Francis Ford Coppola's work bringing Mario Puzo's kinda trashy mobster novel to film and find a film of such craft and care in its construction at every level, all in service towards a central tragedy, that I cannot deny the immense achievement that The Godfather is. It's something of a fulcrum film, vacillating between the precise classical construction that Hollywood had steadily built over decades with the more explicit treatments of sex and violence.

I think one of the reasons this film works so well is that it works both as a family saga and an intimate character portrait, and that they intertwine, interrelate, and inform each other. The saga is of course around the potential fall of the Corleone crime family in New York. Headed by Don Vito (Marlon Brando), the Corleone's are a well-respected family both inside and outside the underworld of the mob. He's spent decades building up contacts around New York, and all of this gets introduced in the bravura opening half hour of the film. It would surprise me if this didn't influence Ingmar Bergman when he made Fanny and Alexander, but the introductory wedding is an amazing piece of filmmaking that bounces from family business, to the business of the wedding, and back, all while introducing at least two dozen characters, all of whom will have their parts to play in the coming drama. The center of it all is the late attendee Michael (Al Pacino), the youngest son of Don Vito, fresh from service in WWII with his girl Kay (Diane Keaton) on his arm. It is through his interactions with her that we get our explicit tellings, like how he explains how Vito got the Frank Sinatra stand-in, Johnny Fontane (Al Martino), out of his limiting contract years ago, by Vito putting a gun to his contract holder's head and saying that either the signature or the brains will be on it. The offer he couldn't refuse. It's also important that Michael says that the story reflects his family but not himself.

Michael is the civilian of the family while everyone else, in particular his two older brothers Sonny (James Caan) and Fredo (John Cazale), are active members of the business. Vito seems to want something different for Michael, which is why he went to college instead of into the business. The irony is that had Sollozzo (Al Lettieri) accepted Vito's answer of no of entering the drug business (he couldn't because Vito had too much singular political control), then Sollozzo might have ended up in a better place. The idea was that Sonny wanted the deal to get into the drug trade, so if Vito is put out of the way, Sonny takes control of the family, and, after a cooling off period from the murder of his father, he'd relinquish control, or enter into a war that he'd fight poorly and lose. If not for Michael, that could have happened, but Michael was simply too cool-headed, to careful, and too vicious to let Sollozzo and his hidden allies in the other five families of New York get away with it.

My father loves this film, and when we'd watch it together when I was young, he liked to point out a specific moment when Michael crosses his legs as the moment he becomes the "godfather", the head of the family. It's in the background of a tracking shot following Sonny, and he has a point. However, there's a moment earlier, when Michael goes to the hospital to visit his father, recovering from Sollozzo's assassination attempt, where Michael takes charge like no one else in the family could, shuffling around a few pieces to create an impression of strength that carries over to the outside world. Is that when he becomes head of the family? No, but it is when he enters the business and shows that he's more capable and smarter than anyone else, and that is a tragedy. It's born of love for his father, to see him simply not murdered, but Michael's intelligence ends up getting put into the service of a crime family where he directs murder.

The most curious part of the film is the central section after Michael kills Sollozzo and the police captain McCluskey (Sterling Hayden) and he retreats to Sicily, a place he'd never lived to survive in hiding under the protection of a local don. It's here where Michael tries to lead a normal life. Having left behind Kay and sacrificed his own life for his family, he tries to settle down with the local girl Apollonia (Simonetta Steganelli), marrying her only to watch her die in an assassination attempt for him. His efforts to help his family have marked him for life, and there's only so running he can do.

The final hour or so of the film is the tragedy unfolding. It's Vito handing control of the family to Michael, the only competent son he has left. It's Michael looking to the future for the family, talking about respectability, but also investing in the drug trade while doing everything behind the scenes to figure out who had backed Sollozzo, who from his own family might have helped, and organizing a move out of the area to start afresh by going west. It's here where Michael's full potential comes forth, and it's terrifying. His cool viciousness comes out, especially in his interactions with Kay. His lies are so easy and backing such a terrible truth while he completely cements his position as the head of a crime family that it's ultimately tragic to see this young man, this veteran of the Second World War, whom his father talked about becoming Senator Corleone, just following in his father's footsteps to become, perhaps, something worse than his father.

As I wrote earlier, the real triumph of this film is the combination of the small scale story of Michael's journey with the larger saga that plays out over a decade from 1945 to 1955 (seriously, years pass between scenes). It's a really intelligent interweaving of interrelated stories as Michael's personal journey influences the saga, giving it deeper meaning, while it goes the other way as well. This approach to the combination of intimate and scale is hardly ever this good in film because it requires a really talented mind to bring it about, and Francis Ford Coppola, result of the Roger Corman system, was that person. The production of Apocalypse Now might have broken his brain, but that was still a few years in the future. This was Coppola making himself known at a scale and with results that make his talent undeniable.

The story is tragic. The craft is impeccable. The acting is perfect. This is a titan of American cinema for a reason.

10.title: The Godfather: A Timeless Masterpiece of Cinema
10.content:
The Godfather is a cinematic masterpiece that continues to stand the test of time. The film's plot follows the Corleone crime family, with particular focus on the patriarch of the family, Vito Corleone, and his son Michael as they navigate their way through the world of organized crime in New York City.

One of the most striking aspects of the film is its ability to blend themes of family, loyalty, power, and corruption in a way that feels both authentic and emotionally resonant. The performances from the cast, particularly Marlon Brando as Vito Corleone and Al Pacino as Michael Corleone, are nothing short of phenomenal and have become iconic in the annals of film history.

Francis Ford Coppola's direction is masterful and the film's score, composed by Nino Rota, perfectly complements the film's mood and atmosphere. The cinematography by Gordon Willis is also noteworthy, capturing the gritty and realistic feel of New York City and the Corleone family's world.

The film's pacing is also well-done, with each scene building on the previous one to create a sense of tension and uncertainty. The editing is seamless and the dialogue is sharp and memorable.

In short, The Godfather is a film that should not be missed. It is a true classic that has left a lasting impact on cinema and popular culture. The film's themes and performances continue to resonate with audiences today and it's no wonder it is considered one of the greatest films ever made.

10.title: The greatest movie of all time
10.content:
The Godfather is an American crime film released in 1972, directed by Francis Ford Coppola, produced by Albert Rudy, screenplay by Coppola and Mario Puzo, and based on the 1969 novel of the same name.

The film stars Marlon Brando and Al Pacino as the leaders of one of New York's most powerful crime families.

The story spans the years 1945-1955, centering around Michael Corleone (Al Pacino)'s transformation from a simple person into a ruthless mafia boss, while also chronicling the Corleone family under the leadership of Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando).

The Godfather is widely considered one of the greatest films in world cinema, and one of the most influential, especially in gangster films. The film is now ranked as the second greatest film in American cinema (after Citizen Kane) by the American Film Institute.

The Godfather was for a while the highest-grossing film of all time, and the highest-grossing film of 1972.

The film won three Oscars out of nine nominations that year: Best Picture, Best Actor for Marlon Brando, and Best Adapted Screenplay for Mario Pozo Francis Coppola.

Nominations for the film in 7 other categories included Al Pacino, James Caan and Robert Duvall for Best Supporting Actor and Francis Coppola for Best Director. The film's success led to the production of The Godfather: Part Two in 1974 and The Godfather: Part Three in 1990.

10.title: The Best Trilogy Ever! May contain spoilers
10.content:
The year is 1945. The Sicilian-American family, the Corleones, is celebrating the wedding of a daughter, Connie, in New York. Everything is going fine...except for the secret meeting held inside the house, a secret meeting on revenge. Don Vito Corleone (Brando) is discussing a problem with a close associate, while his mentor, Tom Hagen (Robert Duvall) stands on. The Don's three sons are outside celebrating the wedding: Sonny, the hot-tempered oldest brother; Fredo, the shy and quiet middle son; and Michael, the youngest son who has returned from fighting in World War II. Sonny and Fredo are in with the Don's council of 'whacking' people, but Michael refuses to be any part of it, due to total commitment to his girlfriend, Kay Adams (Diane Keaton). However, one day while shopping for food with Fredo, Don Corleone is shot by a betrayal, and is rushed to the hospital. The verdict: An assassination attempt. After hearing this, from Long Beach, California, Michael rushes back home to his father. After hearing about the ones who almost killed the Don, he plots revenge with Sonny and close associates. But a twist of fate happens to the family, and in the end, the once-reluctant Michael is made Don over the Corleones.

Francis Ford Coppola beautifully shows a portrait of what seemed to be a harmless family into such malice. The story was adapted from the number one hit by Mario Puzo, who also collaborated with Coppola in this project. The cinematography is excellent, the screenplay gripping and intelligent, and the haunting but enchanting score is memorable. Marlon Brando is absolutely divine as the ruthless, merciful Don Corleone, which earned him the Oscar for Best Actor. New-comer Al Pacino is extremely excellent as Michael, showing both the innocence and fierceness of the son, and his performance received many praises. James Caan is great as scary Sonny, and Robert Duvall could not be a better Tom.

Some notable scenes are the monologue, the Baptism, and the ever-famous horse-head-in-the-bed scene. This demonstrates how scary and malicious the Mob can be. With twists and turns, it shows that even the Mob can lead everyday lives, but one could have a particularly hard time dealing with carrying out a deadly job twenty-four seven.

I personally love this movie, because of the intrigue I felt as I read some of the novel. I definitely recommend this film to people, but I hope that you would not show this to young children. Some things could scar them for life, much like myself...If you like this movie, I also recommend you watch the other two films with the trilogy. In my opinion, this is the greatest trilogy ever made.

`The Godfather' is quite possibly one of the best movies made in history. This film has been quoted/mimicked time and time again, even in a Rugrats (the famous children's cartoon) episode. Why would this movie be quoted so much if it wasn't so amazing? It wouldn't be. All the hype made about this movie really isn't understood until you actually watch the film. 10.title: The Godfather: A Cinematic Masterpiece of Crime and Family
10.content:
"The Godfather," directed by Francis Ford Coppola and based on Mario Puzo's best-selling novel, is a landmark in cinema history. Released in 1972, this film is widely regarded as one of the greatest movies ever made. Its intricate plot, unforgettable characters, and thematic depth have captivated audiences for decades.

The story revolves around the powerful and influential Corleone crime family in post-World War II America. Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) is the patriarch, known as the Godfather, who presides over the family with a mixture of benevolence and ruthless efficiency. His three sons, Sonny (James Caan), Fredo (John Cazale), and Michael (Al Pacino), are positioned to inherit his legacy, though each has a different relationship with the family business.

The film opens with a lavish wedding scene for Vito's daughter, Connie (Talia Shire), establishing the complex web of familial and criminal alliances. This scene masterfully sets the stage for the film's exploration of loyalty, power, and betrayal. Coppola's direction captures the intricate dynamics of the Corleone family and the world they inhabit, weaving a tale that is as much about family bonds as it is about crime and violence.

Marlon Brando's performance as Vito Corleone is iconic, embodying the character's authority and charisma with subtlety and depth. His portrayal won him the Academy Award for Best Actor and remains one of cinema's most memorable roles. Brando's Vito is both a loving family man and a shrewd, calculating leader, exemplifying the dual nature of his character.

Al Pacino's portrayal of Michael Corleone, Vito's youngest son, is equally compelling. Michael starts as a reluctant outsider, a decorated war hero intent on living a life separate from the family business. However, as the story unfolds, Michael is drawn deeper into the criminal underworld, ultimately assuming the role of the family head. Pacino's transformation from the innocent and detached son to a powerful and ruthless leader is one of the film's most captivating arcs. His journey is both tragic and inevitable, showcasing the corrupting influence of power and the demands of loyalty.

The supporting cast, including James Caan as the hot-headed Sonny and Robert Duvall as the loyal consigliere Tom Hagen, delivers exceptional performances that add layers to the film's narrative. The ensemble cast brings to life the complex relationships within the Corleone family, making the audience care deeply about each character's fate.

Coppola's direction, combined with Gordon Willis's cinematography, creates a rich visual tapestry that captures the period and mood of the story. The film's dark, shadowy aesthetic reflects the moral ambiguity and danger inherent in the world of organized crime. Nino Rota's haunting score complements the visuals, enhancing the emotional impact of the story.

The film's exploration of themes such as loyalty, power, and the American Dream resonates with audiences on a universal level. "The Godfather" portrays the criminal underworld as a parallel society with its own rules and hierarchies, examining the fine line between legitimacy and illegality. The Corleone family's struggle for power and survival reflects the broader American experience, questioning the price of ambition and the nature of justice.

One of the film's most famous scenes is the baptism sequence, where Michael stands as godfather to his nephew while orchestrating the brutal elimination of his enemies. This masterful juxtaposition of religious ceremony and violence underscores the film's central themes of duality and moral complexity.

"The Godfather" has left an indelible mark on popular culture, influencing countless films and television shows. Its dialogue, such as Vito's iconic line, "I'm gonna make him an offer he can't refuse," has become part of the cultural lexicon.

In conclusion, "The Godfather" is a cinematic masterpiece that transcends the crime genre to explore profound themes of family, power, and morality. Its compelling characters, masterful storytelling, and timeless themes ensure its place as one of the greatest films ever made. Whether viewed for the first time or revisited, "The Godfather" remains a powerful and unforgettable experience.

10.title: The high praise is well earned
10.content:
Based on the novel by Mario Puzo: in the post-war period of 1945 - 1955 in New York City, Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) leads a criminal family business and is often at war with other Mafia families as well as other enemies. Vito's son, Michael (Al Pacino), wades into the family business and is groomed to eventually lead it.

Director Francis Ford Coppola co-wrote the screenplay with Puzo. The creative team does an excellent job in deceiving the viewer: while we can see that the family does terrible things, we can't help but sympathize with them occasionally especially as they are vulnerable to the acts of other criminal families and betrayals from within the clan. This works mainly due to many scenes involving extended family - the highlight being the enjoyable wedding scene at the film's beginning. The folks we see in such scenes seem to be likeable people.

The acting is brilliant overall with Brando and Pacino standing out. Brando gives a wide-ranging performance especially in the second half where he shows a more mellowing attitude compared to his ways in the first half. And there are many things to praise about Pacino - one of them being his ability to incite terror just by giving a still, brief glare. Pacino also carries the film's mid-section with a series of scenes involving a hospital, a restaurant, and Sicily in that order (a succinct summary). These segments, like others in the film, are intense with perfect build-ups.

The film's most powerful scene involves one where Michael is literally being a godfather at his nephew's baptism. The holy atmosphere of the event is contrasted, back and forth, with other scenes (involving family business) that are anything but holy. The polar opposites play brilliantly against each other in an almost sarcastic way.

And the film ends with a poignant scene between Michael and his wife, Kay (Diane Keaton), and a powerful closing image. A perfect ending for a perfect film.

In addition to the great performances of Pacino, Brando, and Keaton, the excellent cast also includes James Caan, Robert Duvall, Richard Castellano, Sterling Hayden, John Marley, Abe Vigoda, John Cazale, Talia Shire, Gianni Russo, Morgana King, Richard Conte, Lenny Montana and Simonetta Stefanelli.

"The Godfather" is considered outstanding by film critics as well as movie fans. Both groups are right. - dbamateurcritic

Nevertheless, "The Godfather" remains an exceptional film that is unquestionably worth watching. While there may be some minor flaws, they do not detract from the overall quality of the film.
