10.title: As Perfect as Godfather is: No Definitive Version!
10.content:
Godfather and PART II are examples of elite filmmaking. Anyone seeing them for the first time should introduce themselves to the theatrical versions (Part III is good - the Vatican sequences are brilliant - but it's just not in the same league; many scenes were just recaps of what we saw [better] in I & II) ( PART II also recaps some scenes from the original, but they were presented on the "flipside" - and it worked).

Now a very positive gripe: "The Godfather: A Novel for Television" was first broadcast in 1977, it has recently resurfaced on some cable channels (covers I & II in chronological order and retitled The Godfather Saga). What's frustrating is that now, no matter what version I see, I can't help feeling I'm watching an abridged film. For 99.9% of all films, who would care; but this is storytelling at its finest. PART II was innovative for its prequel/sequel presentation that shows (SUBTLE SPOILERS) the irony of the rise and fall of a powerful crime dynasty. But now (I know I'm not alone) after seeing the outakes inserted where they should be, this has made the viewing so much more enriching, especially if you've read Mario Puzo's novel. The problem is that not only is the saga censored (reasonable enough for TV fare), but they've trimmed some lines of dialogue from the theatrical version (I'm not talking about lines containing profanity) apparently for time constraint. What makes the theatrical version more difficult to enjoy now is that the outakes are better pieces of filmaking than 90% of the movies out there (I knew this gripe would turn into a compliment). And in putting it in chronological order, the irony is lessened, but in no way is it lost. The viewer is allowed to see an American tragedy unfold.

I did tape a local broadcast of the "saga" in 1988 and again on AMC recently and both versions of THOSE have little scenes that the other doesn't have. EXAMPLE: At the end of Godfather, the scene fades to black (1955), then fades up to show Michael Corleone (now in 1958) walking along his Nevada lakeside estate in the wee hours of the morning of his son's communion/celebration. It's a well done transition scene that's in the 88' telecast, but not in the recent ones (from a fade to black, it almost jump cuts to the party and Fredo's entrance with wife Deanna). Even the bonus disc of the DVD that contains deleted scenes (separate from the films) don't contain all of them. Just one example is (from Godfather I), the first scene that introduces Don Corleone, after the undertaker Bonasera exits the Don's study, Sonny is sternly chastised by the Don for not paying attention (that was worth seeing just to hear Marlon Brando whistle). It's duration is only about 10 seconds long, but it cements the fact that Sonny is the intended Don in training who still needs tweaking by his father.

This is damn fine filmmaking that captures the texture and atmosphere of the time told in the story; be it early 1900's, mid 40's thru the late 50's and Coppola successfully borrowed from the styles of moviemaking, styles lifted from the 20's, 40's and 50's. Movies over 50 years ago didn't have fancy subjective camera moves and Coppola's decision to film using old fashion techniques makes you feel you're watching a film from that time era (I realize this was early 70's, but new wave style and zip zooms had been around for 10 years[?] ).

I'm confident that hundreds of thousands (millions ?) of movie lovers would immerse themselves in a longer UNCUT version that is no longer constrained by theatrical time factors. 7 hours and 15 minutes (not including end credits and no Part III) would be impossible in a theater, but this is the age of home entertainment (still can't beat watching a movie in the theater) that allows freedom AND a stop button (2 or 3 well placed intermissions would be better). That means you're saddled with more footage of Al Pacino, Marlon Brando, Robert DeNiro, Robert Duvall, James Caan, John Cazale, Diane Keaton, Talia Shire...ect giving us some of the finest performances in their careers. Any complaints about that?? Special mention to all but especially James Caan who lost so much footage to the cutting room floor. During the 2nd act of the Godfather, James Caan and Al Pacino are the stars of the movie as the story flips back and forth between the two; after all Sonny is the heir apparent. To show how instrumental he was to the family by exposing his leadership ability and softer side made what follows that much more shocking.

No, I didn't buy the DVD (I did rent the bonus disc) for these reasons. I'll wait till they reconstruct the saga on a new DVD edition(if rumors are true) but please...no Part III.

(Subtle Spoiler) Note: Never was comfortable when Godfather PART II changed Vito's birthday from April 28,1887 (The Godfather -cemetery monument) to 1892 (from the opening "In 1901 the godfather was born Vito...he was nine years old!) Marlon Brando's closing scenes led you to believe the 1887 birthdate.

Francis Coppola is an artistic genius, he's never made up his mind to stop tinkering with editing the saga. Even the Godfather Epic 1902-1959 contained only some deleted scene and excised 2 or 3 scenes from the theatrical version. I'm looking forward to THE version where all the scenes are left intact.

The Godfather 10 out of 10 The Godfather PART II 10 out of 10 The Godfather Saga (uncensored) a 10+

10.title: Lessons for Men
10.content: I'd like to preface this by acknowledging that my rating does somewhat reinforce the male stereotype pointed out in Greta Gerwig's Barbie. But there just is something that men find fascinating about this franchise. My introduction to this movie itself comes from a close friend of mine's enthusiasm for the movie, I will come back to the meaning the movie has to men. I was not very familiar with Francis Ford Coppola's work but this movie has pointed out to me that this may very much have been a mistake. The very first scene, caught my eye from a directing standpoint, the slow zooming out whilst Bonasera explains his situation to the Don Corleone makes it very clear the influence and power that the godfather has. And accompanying this filming prowess throughout, is an absolutely beautiful score that well deserved its withdrawn Academy Award. The touches of Italian culture throughout the movie almost makes me long for Italian heritage, which is an homage to how beautifully it was implemented in the film. The acting in this film is near flawless and makes the viewing immersive, I found myself rooting for the Corleone family almost as if I were part of it. Marlon Brando's presence on screen, as always, is marvelous. To add to that, Al Pacino's depiction of Micheal Corleone's character development is frictionless and coherent with the events that happen throughout. Talia Shire's performance translates perfectly the emotions Connie would be feeling especially when she confronts her brother. I could go on and on about the brilliant show of acting in this movie, but I want to focus on the meaning the film has. I am but a sub-par movie reviewer and most likely will not have picked up on any ground-breaking imagery never before highlighted, but I am here to talk about why this movie speaks to men in a way few pieces of art do. Micheal Corleone start his life somewhat distancing himself from his family's business due to his different moral compass, something many can relate to, it can be very easy to look at others lives and think we would act differently given the chance, and similarly, young men may start their lives thinking they have a perfect record. But there comes a time when we have to step up, when duty comes knocking at the door, you may have no choice but to answer. When the Sollozzo tried to have Vito killed, Micheal had no choice but to step up and organise to have his father avenged. It is this acceptance of current situations which makes him become the man he is at the end of the movie. You will be challenged in life, and when you do, you must take matters into your own hands, you can try to make excuses, you can try to blame it on other factors but eventually you will have to come to terms with the fact that things are the way they are and it is only up to you to change them. There are many notable quotes about family in this movie, "A man who doesn't spend time with family, can never be a real man." - Vito Corleone, "Never tell anybody outside the family what you're thinking again." - Vito Corleone, "Don't ever take sides with anyone against the family again. Ever." - Micheal Corleone. Which all partly summarise a broader message that blood is thicker than water, no questions asked. Men resonate with that message for their own personal reasons, but one thing they almost all have in common, they will, for the most part, be fathers of children, husbands of wives and godfather to godsons and for some, the don of their extended family too. All of these commitments connect to legacy and continuity beyond their own life, and for that commitment to not go in vain, there must be a passed down value which prioritises family, always. Words to live by.

Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather is a cinematic masterpiece that has captivated audiences for decades. This epic crime drama delves into the intricate world of the Corleone family, a powerful Mafia clan led by the enigmatic Don Vito Corleone.

The film masterfully portrays the rise and fall of the Corleone family through the eyes of its youngest son, Michael Corleone. As Michael reluctantly becomes embroiled in the family business, he undergoes a transformation from a war hero to a ruthless crime lord.

One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its complex characters. 10.title: A movie critic's dream.
10.content:
"The Godfather" is one of the most praised movies in cinema history. It gives everything that critics and audiences alike ask for in movies. In my opinion it gets all the attention it gets for being one of, or the best movies ever. One of the best things "The Godfather" does is its incredible casting and its iconic performances from each and every one of its characters. The actors are so convincing that it won the movie several academy awards. It also jumpstarted several actors, acting careers, and gave an incredible ending to others. The Characters in the movie are outstandingly well handled. Each Character has somewhat of an arc within themselves, it shows each of their worldview and opinion of the situation that they face. It shows how their opinions, worldview, and personalities conflict with each other, and the consequences for reckless, illogical, and sudden decisions made by various characters. The film also gives the greatest character arc literally ever, through Michael Coralone, played by the incredible Al Pacino. The Godfather takes the viewer behind the closed doors of the Coralone crime family, a powerful Italian mafia group, and explores the pros and Cons of the organized crime lifestyle. Somehow through the immoral lifestyle that this movie bases itself upon, through things like narcotics, prostitution, alcohol, and violence it deals with very evident moral issues that we still face today, and does it in a somewhat redeemable way. The movie is also able to maintain a complex story with several moving parts, while also developing a very slow paced story. Therefore it spends time to dissect and flesh out its Characters and plot. It gives you a lot of time to interact and emotionally connect with its Characters, so that when they are lost it leaves a lasting impact on the viewer, and changes your view on the movie, and shows how it affects each of the characters involved differently. Another one of my favorite components of the Godfather is the cinematography and atmosphere. Its usage of crucial elements such as casting shadows and lighting communicates the dark essence that the film is going for, culture, and immorality, but always is able to communicate a sense of hope throughout. "The Godfather" has a very accurate portrayal of Italian culture and ways that culture is established within Immigrant America. I really enjoyed the cinematic representation visualization of organized crime and the abundance of style throughout. Speaking of style, another way the film communicates style and Italian culture is through the score. Just like the cinematography, the score communicates style and Italian culture, and accurately represents the way we visualize culture, crime, and atmosphere. "The Godfather" holds the best and most detailed character arc I have ever seen. You experience progressive stages of complete transformation through the changes of worldview and personality over the long period of time that this film takes place in.

"The Godfather" though a very great movie, is very slow moving, so those who prefer their movies to be modern and fast paced fast paced may take a disliking to this movie. The Godfather has stood the test of time and leaves a lasting impact on cinema still today. It wows critics and audiences alike, and will for years to come. It truly is one of the greatest films ever produced.

10.title: Close, but not the greatest
10.content: "The Godfather" is a visceral achievement in moviemaking and has a rightful place near the top of any list of the greatest films ever made. It seizes your attention, doesn't let go and takes you down the road promised to immigrants to America -- before taking a turn in which we confront the prejudices, mistrust and other roadblocks to the realization of their dreams, and how they went on to create success on their terms. But I have to put it near the top, not AT the top. That honor, on my list, belongs to "The Godfather Part II," for a reason that it's hard to fault Coppola for. In "The Godfather," I found Michael to be too far outside the family at the beginning of the movie. While not renouncing his father, Sonny or their enterprise, Michael seems to be more of an observer in an Army uniform with his white-bread girlfriend nearby than a family member PLANNING to immerse himself in the life his father and brother have chosen. Obviously Michael is drawn closer to his family as it becomes threatened with, then targeted by, violence. This is understandable but, to me, not foreshadowed by the life outside the family that he had chosen a few years earlier and seemed to be comfortable with. Of course, "Part II" gives a much fuller picture of how Michael got to where he was in running the enterprise, and heading the family. But we already know all we need to know about his motives and choices -- courtesy of "The Godfather." This deeper, more realized character of Michael in "Part II" is the reason I rate it ahead of "The Godfather" -- but not by much.

10.title: A Timeless Masterpiece: The Godfather
10.content:
The Godfather," directed by Francis Ford Coppola, stands as a cinematic masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences worldwide. Released in 1972, this iconic film has earned its reputation as one of the finest works in the history of cinema. Its compelling narrative, unforgettable characters, and impeccable craftsmanship make it an enduring classic.

Plot and Storyline: "The Godfather" delves into the complex world of the Corleone family, a formidable Italian-American Mafia dynasty led by the enigmatic Vito Corleone, portrayed brilliantly by Marlon Brando. The narrative explores themes of power, loyalty, betrayal, and honor within the context of organized crime. Adapted from Mario Puzo's novel, the screenplay weaves a rich and multi-dimensional narrative that keeps viewers engaged throughout.

Characters and Performances: The film boasts an ensemble cast that delivers iconic performances. Marlon Brando's portrayal of Vito Corleone is a masterclass in acting, and Al Pacino's transformation from a reluctant outsider to a formidable mafia boss as Michael Corleone is truly mesmerizing. The supporting cast, including James Caan and Robert Duvall, offer outstanding performances that add depth and authenticity to the characters.

Direction and Cinematography: Francis Ford Coppola's direction is a work of art in itself. His meticulous attention to detail, use of symbolism, and ability to create tension through silence are unparalleled. The cinematography by Gordon Willis is equally remarkable, with its dark, moody visuals setting the perfect tone for the film's dark and complex narrative.

Music and Score: Nino Rota's haunting score is unforgettable and enhances the film's atmosphere. The "Godfather Theme" has become an instantly recognizable piece of cinematic music that perfectly complements the film's gravitas.

Legacy and Impact: "The Godfather" has left an indelible mark on the film industry, serving as a source of inspiration for countless filmmakers, writers, and actors. Its exploration of power, family, and morality continues to resonate with audiences today, and its cultural influence extends well beyond the movie theater.

10.title: Perfection.
10.content:
"The Godfather" is a pinnacle of cinematographic excellence, evident in its meticulous attention to detail and masterful execution. Three specific examples highlight the film's brilliance:

The Opening Scene: The film's iconic opening sequence sets the tone for the entire narrative. As Amerigo Bonasera pleads for justice for his daughter, the camera slowly zooms in on his face, capturing every flicker of emotion in Marlon Brando's performance. The use of close-up shots emphasizes the intensity of Bonasera's desperation, while the stark lighting creates a sense of foreboding. This scene establishes the film's themes of power, loyalty, and justice, laying the foundation for the story that unfolds.

The Wedding Sequence: The wedding scene is a masterclass in visual storytelling, showcasing Francis Ford Coppola's ability to orchestrate complex ensemble shots. The sprawling mise-en-scène captures the opulence of the Corleone family's world, with the camera weaving through the crowd, introducing key characters and relationships. The use of long takes and fluid camera movements creates a sense of intimacy and immersion, drawing viewers into the festivities. Meanwhile, subtle details in the background, such as the whispered conversations and exchanged glances, hint at the underlying tensions simmering beneath the surface.

The Restaurant Murder: One of the most iconic scenes in cinematic history, the restaurant murder is a tour de force of suspense and tension. Shot from Michael Corleone's perspective, the scene unfolds in real-time, intensifying the sense of immediacy and danger. The use of low-key lighting and deep shadows heightens the atmosphere of dread, while the absence of music accentuates the sound of the train rumbling overhead. As Michael calmly executes his plan, the camera remains steady, capturing every calculated movement and expression. The scene's shocking climax, punctuated by the sudden eruption of violence, leaves an indelible impression on viewers, solidifying "The Godfather" as a cinematic masterpiece.

10.title: You straightened my brother out?
10.content:
What an absolutely marvelous movie! Ford Coppola is truly an amazing director, and so are the entire cast of The Godfather. If it weren't for the second film of this franchise, and also Goodfellas, I would've undoubtedly dubbed this as the best crime drama of all time.

The movie starts out showing the full and yet uncorrupted Corleone family, with Don Vito Corleone as the head of the family, Sonny as the hot headed underboss, Tom Hagen as the Consigliere, Fredo as the weak brother who is something between a soldier and a capo and Michael, the youngest of them all who doesn't want to walk along the path of his father. Soon enough though, internal trust issues arise in the family as multiple assasination attempts are carried out on a few family members, of which, Michael takes revenge for.

In an attempt to hide Michael from the ensuing drama, he is sent back to Sicily, where he finds new life and tries to start from there. But his short yet dark history follows him and he is left with nothing after going through all the things he has gone through. The innocent, brave war hero Michael is now willing to take on his father's shoes and bring the Corleone family its lost muscle and respect.

In this movie, we see many things that current movie crews can learn from. From using lighting to cover heavy make-up, to an absolute masterful execution of a Juxtaposition right around the end, this movie has it all. All 3 hours of it is a beautiful learning and enjoyable experience.

Also just saying, if you're watching this with kids, there's just a few seconds of upper-body nudity here from Simonetta Stefanelli and that's about it. So if your kid is above 14-15 it should be fine.

The story of the Corleone family is both gripping and emotional, focusing not just on crime but on themes of family, loyalty, and power. The transformation of Michael Corleone, played by Al Pacino, is particularly powerful. He starts off as someone who wants nothing to do with the family business but ends up becoming its ruthless leader. Watching that change is fascinating.

Marlon Brando's performance as Don Vito Corleone is also unforgettable. He's both intimidating and caring, and his character feels real and complex. The film has many iconic moments, like Michael's first kill in the restaurant and the famous line, "I'll make him an offer he can't refuse." These scenes are tense, well-acted, and memorable.

The pacing of the movie is slow but intentional, allowing viewers to really immerse themselves in the world Coppola has created. The dark, moody cinematography and the haunting score by Nino Rota add to the overall atmosphere, making the film visually and emotionally impactful.

The Godfather isn't just a typical gangster movie. It's a deep, thoughtful film that explores what people are willing to do for family and power. It's a movie that stays with you long after you've finished watching it, and for me, it's an all-time favorite.

10.content:
"The Godfather," directed by Francis Ford Coppola, is nothing short of a cinematic triumph. Released in 1972, this film has stood the test of time and remains a benchmark for excellence in filmmaking. Adapted from Mario Puzo's novel, it tells the engrossing tale of the powerful Corleone crime family, blending intricate storytelling with top-tier performances.

Marlon Brando delivers an iconic performance as Vito Corleone, the patriarchal head of the family. His portrayal is both subdued and commanding, exuding a quiet power that leaves an indelible mark on the audience. Al Pacino, as Michael Corleone, showcases a masterful transformation from a war-hero outsider to a ruthless mafia leader. The cast, including James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Diane Keaton, all contribute to the film's undeniable gravitas.

The screenplay is nothing short of genius. It intricately weaves themes of loyalty, power, betrayal, and family into a narrative that is as compelling as it is complex. Coppola's direction is meticulous and layered, allowing the story to unfold at a deliberate yet engaging pace. The cinematography by Gordon Willis adds a rich, almost operatic quality to the film, with its use of shadows and light contributing to a sense of impending doom.

Nino Rota's haunting score complements the film perfectly, enhancing the emotional weight of key scenes and contributing to its timeless quality.

What sets "The Godfather" apart is its ability to humanize its characters, even as it portrays a world steeped in crime and violence. It tells a universally resonant story about power and its influence on the human condition. The film is also a brilliant exploration of the immigrant experience, showing the lengths to which individuals will go to protect their family and secure their legacy.

"The Godfather" is more than just a movie; it is an experience, a study in cinematic excellence that has influenced countless films and storytellers. Its meticulous craftsmanship, stellar performances, and profound narrative make it a must-watch for any film enthusiast. Over four decades later, it continues to reign supreme as one of the greatest films ever made.

In closing, "The Godfather" is an essential piece of cinema that captures the essence of storytelling at its finest, and its impact will undoubtedly resonate for generations to come.

Review of "The Godfather"

Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather," released in 1972, is a cinematic masterpiece that has secured its place as one of the greatest films ever made. Based on Mario Puzo's novel of the same name, this epic crime drama captivates audiences with its powerful storytelling, memorable characters, and profound exploration of power, family, and morality within the Mafia underworld of 1940s and 50s America.

At the heart of "The Godfather" is the Corleone crime family, led by the iconic Don Vito Corleone, played flawlessly by Marlon Brando. Brando's portrayal of the aging patriarch is nothing short of legendary, capturing both the ruthless determination and tender familial love that define the character. His raspy voice and imposing presence command every scene he is in, making Don Vito a figure of both fear and admiration.

Al Pacino delivers a career-defining performance as Michael Corleone, the youngest son who initially wants nothing to do with his family's criminal enterprises. Pacino's transformation from a reluctant outsider to a ruthless leader is portrayed with subtle intensity, showcasing his character's moral descent as he becomes increasingly embroiled in the world of organized crime.

The supporting cast is equally exceptional, with James Caan as the hotheaded Sonny Corleone, Robert Duvall as the pragmatic Tom Hagen, and Diane Keaton as Michael's innocent wife, Kay Adams. Each actor brings depth and complexity to their roles, adding layers to the intricate web of relationships and betrayals that drive the narrative forward.

Coppola's direction is masterful, employing a deliberate pace that allows the characters and their motivations to unfold naturally. The film's cinematography, by Gordon Willis, is striking, using shadow and light to heighten the drama and emphasize the moral ambiguity of the characters' actions. The score, composed by Nino Rota, is hauntingly beautiful, underscoring the film's emotional weight and dramatic tension.

10.title: what a great movie !
10.content:
"The Godfather" is a cinematic masterpiece that stands as a towering achievement in film history. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola and based on Mario Puzo's novel, the movie delves deep into the complexities of family, power, and loyalty within the Italian-American mafia.

Marlon Brando delivers an iconic performance as Vito Corleone, the aging patriarch whose authority is unquestioned, yet he carries himself with a quiet dignity that demands respect. His portrayal earned him an Academy Award for Best Actor, and it's easy to see why. Brando's Don Corleone is both formidable and endearing, a leader who rules not just through fear, but through a deep sense of familial obligation.

Al Pacino's transformation as Michael Corleone is equally compelling. Starting as the family's outsider, his journey into the heart of the family business is marked by a series of calculated decisions that reveal a cold and calculating mind. Pacino brings a nuanced depth to Michael, showcasing his evolution from war hero to ruthless mafia boss.

The film's narrative is a brutal sweep of magnificent storytelling, seamlessly blending stomach-turning violence with moments of profound intimacy. It reinvents the mobster genre, presenting its characters not as caricatures, but as deeply flawed individuals caught in a web of tradition and ambition.

Coppola's direction is meticulous, creating an atmosphere that is both grand and intimate. The wedding scene alone is a marvel of filmmaking, introducing characters and dynamics with a richness that many films struggle to achieve in their entirety.

The cinematography and Nino Rota's score work in harmony to evoke a period setting that has aged remarkably well. The film paces itself deliberately, allowing its moments of action and horror to resonate all the more powerfully.

In summary, "The Godfather" is not just a gangster film; it's a poignant study of the human condition, a saga of a family that, despite its criminal dealings, is relatable in its struggles and desires. It's a film that has left an indelible mark on cinema and continues to influence filmmakers and audiences alike.

"The Godfather" is a cinematic masterpiece that has established itself as one of the greatest films in history. Released in 1972 and directed by Francis Ford Coppola, the movie captivates audiences with its gripping narrative, unforgettable characters, and remarkable performances.

Set in the world of organized crime, "The Godfather" follows the Corleone family, led by patriarch Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) and his sons Michael (Al Pacino), Sonny (James Caan), and Fredo (John Cazale). The film delves into the intricate workings of the mafia, exploring themes of power, family, loyalty, and the consequences of a life surrounded by violence.

What makes "The Godfather" truly exceptional is its ability to create a rich and immersive atmosphere, transporting viewers into the dark underbelly of the mafia. The film beautifully captures the essence of the 1940s and 1950s, with meticulous attention to detail in terms of set design, costumes, and cinematography. The haunting score composed by Nino Rota adds another layer of depth to the storytelling, perfectly complementing the on-screen events.

The performances in "The Godfather" are nothing short of extraordinary. Marlon Brando delivers an iconic portrayal of Vito Corleone, for which he won an Academy Award. Al Pacino, in his breakout role as Michael Corleone, showcases his incredible range as an actor, transforming from an innocent young man to a calculating and ruthless leader. The supporting cast, including James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Diane Keaton, all contribute immensely to the film's brilliance.

Beyond its gripping narrative and impeccable performances, "The Godfather" presents a thought-provoking exploration of morality and the corrupting nature of power. It raises profound questions about the choices individuals make and the consequences they face in a world where honor and loyalty hold immense significance.

It is now past 1 PM and I just finished watching Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather". I should probably go to bed. It's late and tomorrow I have to wake up a bit early. But not early enough to postpone writing these lines. Now that I have seen it three times, the opportunity of sharing my thoughts and refreshed insights are too much of a good offer to sit on. So, bear with me.

This film works so well because it takes place in an underworld in which we are so embedded that we do not even observe it. Coppola puts us straight in the smack-dab center of what is, admittedly, a society made by criminals for criminals. It is also the reason why it's so welcoming. We are surrounded by its inhabitants--cold-blooded murderers, men who see crime like a 9 to 5 job masquerading as honorable men. And I do mean men. From the outside, we would only witness the horrifying, disturbing manifestations of their well-thought out actions.

But it goes even deeper than that. It all revolves around the Corleone family led by Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). He is the most honest of these men, sitting right on the edge. But for people like him, who do not fully embrace this world, it's not easy. He avoids conflict until it is absolutely necessary. He is a man defined by moral principles. There is a scene at the beginning, in which, during his daughter's wedding day, one of his associates, Luca Brasi (Lenny Montana) practices his speech that he is going to give to the Don when he meets him. The scene with these two is funny and almost adorable. I could not help but sympathize both of them only to realize that I am feeling warmth for two mobsters. Not to even mention that Lenny Montana was an actual mob hit-man and that he was actually nervous as he said that line.

The more I watched the more I realized just how incredibly com.

10.title: Still at the top of my list
10.content:
The Godfather was an epic novel, an excellent story, and the movie could have easily been botched on numerous levels; instead, Francis Ford Coppola managed to create an enduring masterpiece of modern cinema. This excellence he achieved in spite of the constant harassment and general incompetence of Paramount Pictures. Coppola was almost fired by the studio several times during the filming of this classic, yet he managed to persevere and realize his vision through to the end. The casting, direction, acting, cinematography, and story are all top notch. Add to it a beautiful score by Nino Rota and you have the #1 IMDb movie of all time. This is a movie I have watched many times and found few weaknesses.

If Paramount had its way, The Godfather would have been much different. In this alternate reality, Coppola would have been fired and replaced with some studio sycophant director. There would be no Marlon Brando as Vito Corleone, since Paramount felt Brando was a troublemaker. Michael would have been played by Ryan O'Neal or Robert Redford since Paramount wanted a "prettier" leading man. Al Pacino, despite superior acting ability, would have probably remained undiscovered. The story would not have taken place in the 40's and 50's, but instead would have been contemporary in order to minimize production costs. To be sure, the ultimate result of Paramount's expediency would have been unmitigated disaster. Thankfully, Coppola fought Paramount throughout the entire production, and much like the Godfather himself, refused to dance on the strings of those Paramount pezzonovante.

It reserves itself and only gets brutal/intense when necessary, and even the most simple and quiet of scenes have an immense sense of meaning to them. The acting was phenomenal, the rapport between characters was so visceral and real and despite being the furthest thing from a mobster, I cared so deeply for these characters and their family.

10.title: The Don of all movies
10.content:
It is widely known that 'The Godfather' is one of the five or ten greatest movies ever conceived. About three months ago, it celebrated its 50th anniversary, and was beautifully restored by a group of immensely talented people. I saw the film at a special screening at the Paramount lot theater, and it was one of the best experiences I've ever had watching a movie. Not only was I illuminated and electrified by the masterpiece up there on the screen, but I was also admiring how great the movie both looked and felt. I had always known that the film had become grainy, and even the first time I saw it I could tell. The restoration makes it look just about flawless.

It's a flawless movie, a life changing movie, a film changing movie... it's a movie with composure that Coppola hasn't lived up to since, or for that matter, I don't think any director has since. Coppola's direction is so precise, concise, efficient, lean and organized, and has beautifully intertwined pacing. If it's not the best movie I've ever seen, then it's certainly the most beautifully choreographed, wonderfully paced I've ever seen.

The beautifully constructed and rich plot follows Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando), the Don of a postwar organized crime family, who's getting older and older. After a series of complicated events, his leadership shifts to the youngest of the family, Michael (Al Pacino). At first, Michael is hesitant to break into such brooding and dark territory, but slowly transforms into somebody that he thought he'd never be. The cast also includes James Caan, Diane Keaton, Richard S. Castellano, Robert Duvall, Sterling Hayden, John Marley, Richard Conte, Abe Vigoda, Talia Shire, John Cazale, and Lenny Montana.

Every sequence is designed with such passion and craft that it is hard to not be completely sucked in. My favorite scenes are the wedding sequence at the beginning, which Coppola intertwines with meetings with the Don, and the scenes with Capt. McCluskey, a corrupt police captain, eating dinner with Michael. I will not spoil anything. I think this is a film that everybody must see. It is an element of modern art; little has achieved such a high status. It's unquestionably a masterpiece, and a movie that brought American popular entertainment to the ranks of the foreign masters. It was a joy to see it again and absorb so much.

It's probably the best movie I've ever seen.

10.title: A Personal Anecdote

I remember before I'd even seen the movie, I heard talk of it, especially the horse head scene. I would have been about fifteen years old, and although I can't even remember when I saw the film for the first time. I remember how everyone in the world was reading the novel back then, as people used to do, you know, read. The series also talks a lot about the movie Love Story, another film that came from a novel that EVERYONE was reading back then.

I have nothing new to say about The Godfather except to throw in a personal anecdote.

This must have been back in about 1989 on a Thursday evening. We were at a friend's house; I think we were three couples. We were having a beer before going out with The Godfather on the TV. We'd all seen it countless times by then, but we found ourselves riveted once again. We weren't in any big hurry to leave with nothing important going on that night, certainly nothing more important than watching this great film for the umpteenth time.

We may have already had our coats on when the film approached the pivotal moment when Michael is taken to the Louis Italian-American Restaurant when the screen went blank and a message appeared: To Be Continued Tomorrow Evening. We all let out a gasp. Then we took decisive action.

One of us headed out to the video store (remember those?), someone else went out for beer and wine, and someone ordered pizza. We stayed in and watched the second half. Who needs to go out?

10.title: One of the greatest of all time
10.content:
This film works so well because it takes place in an underworld in which we are so embedded that we do not even observe it. Coppola puts us straight in the smack-dab center of what is, admittedly, a society made by criminals for criminals. It is also the reason why it's so welcoming. We are surrounded by its inhabitants--cold-blooded murderers, men who see crime like a 9 to 5 job masquerading as honorable men. And I do mean men. From the outside, we would only witness the horrifying, disturbing manifestations of their well-thought out actions.

But it goes even deeper than that. It all revolves around the Corleone family led by Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). He is the most honest of these men, sitting right on the edge. But for people like him, who do not fully embrace this world, it's not easy. He avoids conflict until it is absolutely necessary. He is a man defined by moral principles. There is a scene at the beginning, in which, during his daughter's wedding day, one of his associates, Luca Brasi (Lenny Montana) practices his speech that he is going to give to the Don when he meets him. The scene with these two is funny and almost adorable. I could not help but sympathize both of them only to realize that I am feeling warmth for two mobsters. Not to even mention that Lenny Montana was an actual mob hit-man and that he was actually nervous as he said that line.

10.title: A perfect movie in every aspect.

What can I say, an outstanding movie, certainly the best that I have ever seen.

The Godfather depicts organised crime in a way that no other film ever has, or ever will. Although there is violence, it is put in very discretely- instead choosing to focus on the Italian family values that the Godfather and his heir, Michael, have adopted. It is a beautiful portrait of a seemingly happy family, with dark secrets. Eventually, the family suffers because of their underworld status, and Michael Corleone eventually takes over the family, with all of his father's wisdom, but with the ruthlessness of his late brother. The direction and the acting of the Michael character is exceptional. Al Pacino portrays him perfectly, and Francis Ford Coppola masterfully directed his transition from family rebel and sweet Westernised man to aggressive and ruthless kingpin of the family business.

The music is another pivotal part of the movie. Nino Rota's famous main theme of the Godfather will stick in anybody's head for the remainder of their life. The lighting is also very well done, with the dark orange colour which adds to the overall effect of the movie.

All in all, a brilliant masterpiece, with no flaws whatsoever, 10 out of 10.

10.title: The Coppola Restoration
10.content:
The name "The Coppola Restoration" says it all - because the complete "Godfather" trilogy for this Blu-ray edition has been extensively restored at the insistence of director Francis Ford Coppola. Since the original camera negative no longer existed, the best possible pieces were brought together from all parts of the world, subjected to film scanning on a 4k scanner and then polished on thousands of individual images using the latest digital technology: Contrast and colors were optimized and coordinated with one another , Dirt particles removed and much more.

All this and what Steven Spielberg has to do with the whole thing can be found in the article "Rescue through film emulsion", which is unfortunately a bit short at 19 minutes. "When the shooting was over" also focuses on technical processes such as editing and music. Indispensable for cineastes is "A masterpiece that was almost none", which addresses the difficult production conditions and the problematic situation of the filmmakers at the end of the sixties (with detailed input from George Lucas, among others). The pop-cultural meaning of "The Godfather" is made abundantly clear to the viewer in "The Godfather's World" (keyword "The Simpsons"). In addition, there are many other new bonuses and - kudos to Paramount - all the extras of the DVD edition from 2001 (including three frank director's comments, a 75-minute documentary, deleted scenes). Our conclusion: the Blu-ray box is an offer that cannot be refused.

10.title: The complete package, representative at the top of cinematography
10.content:
As my title suggests, I believe the Godfather and specifically the first part is arguably the most complete movie in the top 250 in that all its elements are of high quality - the story, the characters, the presentation techniques such as lighting. It is masterfully adapted from a definitely well-written novel and it's obvious that the movie producers also followed and emphasised the themes the writer focused on appropiately.

The plot is interesting. Many characters with different yet realistic and engaging personalities, also portrayed brilliantly by the actors and commonly found in mafia contexts, do their part in what is a multi-way fight for power in the underground world. That obviously comes with sufficient action and drama, tense moments and top quality suspense in many moments, some more surprising than others (e.g. Solozzo getting shot vs Apollonia getting exploded).

The movie (and book therefore) include many moments which are at the border between being too extreme & obviously from a fictional movie, and being believable and even realistic. I think this is not a bad thing, movies contribute to our entertainment and getting away from the more mundane real world, not all has to be ruthlessly realistic but it sure has to be believable and the Godfather is just that.

For me, questions have to be asked about its depth and true intentions. Is it just a mafia movie about mobsters shooting each other, or is it a rollercoaster of emotions in which we are asked to think and reflect upon deep themes? It's more the first option than the second for me. The main masterful theme executed in this movie and certainly in the second part is Michael's character development and how he gets caught up in the "family business". A seemingly kind and relatively soft-spoken young man having to help his family in mafia business in a difficult moment. The old boss, his dad, gets targeted and he feels he has to act, to protect, and eventually to get revenge. All this leads him down a path of narcissistic desire to be in control of everything. It also transforms him into a paranoid and ruthless dictator ordering the execution of anyone that is a threat, and that transition is finalised in the next part when that ends up applying to his own family members. Michael's psychology is quite interesting and understandable and it's definitely been analysed a lot throughout the years, and I feel he is the trilogy's main focus and the thing that gives the movie most of its depth and potential to be reflected upon.

The rest, whilst many characters are great, interesting, different, realistic, well-acted, and each have their own intricacies, backstories and tasks to do in the movie, they end up feeling simply like tools to execute this mafia show that don't really have a higher meaning. Marlon Brando, though, I can only applaud that performance, it's just so fun to watch any scene involving him even if it's just sitting and talking. The depth of his character comes mostly from his personality and status/position. You start wondering what he went through that he acts like that, and how he got there.

Needless to say, the narrative is compelling, and there are indeed only very few/small flaws in its execution. The brilliant aspects and quality of its elements and storytelling make up for them a thousand times over. Definitely one of my favorites.

10.title: What happens if you step into Chaos?
10.content:
When you finally decide to watch this movie, since it came out in the 70s, and you were born about twenty years later, you sit down in front of your TV with some degree of expectation. Expectation the movie sees in your eyes, then laughs at you for some minutes. And then a man wakes up with blood all over his pajamas and a horse head in his bed. So you realise that something you were simply fearing is actually true. That is the complex life of the Corleone family.

But please, try ignoring your expectations. Forget about the hype, as many describe this as one of the "greatest movies of all time", if not THE one. You won't be disappointed, that is, but there is nothing like a "greatest" movie. This is "only" a masterpiece in cinematographic production, acting, writing and score, much akin to an opera piece.

"The Godfather" does not care about classical Aristotelian unity, and it can do that thanks to an incredibly coherent screenplay thanks to the combined effort of writer Mario Puzo and director F.F. Coppola. Years pass by, oceans are crossed and decisions are taken without the viewers noticing, as they can't ignore every character's intriguing motivations and cold-hearted yet realistic resolution. This is one of the greatest strenghts of the movie, as its surrealisticly realistic tone constantly entangles your brain in its world: you always know that all you are watching is just fiction, only a story, yet it impossible for the viewer to unsee the cruel nature of a world that did exist. Its a "historical character saga" about nonexistent characers.

Marlon Brando's and Al Pacino's performances have no particular traints of features. Because they are flawless. The supporting cast did a great job too, so good in fact that most of the time you can't tell who is the supporting and who's the main cast.

Gordon Willis' fotography is gorgeous from the first moments of the movie. Slowly moving scenes, beautifully lit like Caravaggio's portraits, bring a whole new life to the words "noir" and "chiaroscuro". We are talking about Italians, after all, and making Marlon Brando mumble some "italian" words sure does not mean a lot. Still, it was nice to hear Italian words pronounced correctly almost all the time.

Nino Rota did not write music. The sophisticated sounds you hear while your eyes are accompanied by the splendidly crafted frames are powerful overflows of emotions. Nino Rota was truly a prodigy and a master of his art.

But how are all these different features kept toghether in this masterpiece of a movie? It's a slow and steady descent into darkness, just look at Al Pacino's character, Michele Corleone. So, what happens if you finally step into chaos? Well, you won't like it. Your life won't like it. Your loved ones won't like it. But you won't even notice.

10.title: An Eternal Masterpiece
10.content:
The Godfather is a cinematic masterpiece that has etched its name in the annals of film history. With profound impact, this film has managed to touch the souls of audiences from various generations. The Godfather is widely regarded as one of the greatest films of all time, and there is no doubt that it stands as a monumental achievement in the world of cinema.

First and foremost, the reason why The Godfather is so impressive lies in the extraordinary quality of its performances. Marlon Brando's portrayal of Don Vito Corleone is unforgettable, with charisma and emotional depth that truly embody the character. Al Pacino's performance as Michael Corleone is equally astounding, showcasing an incredible character transformation from the beginning to the end of the film. Not only the main cast, but also the supporting actors like James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Diane Keaton deliver brilliant contributions that make this film truly exceptional.

The screenplay of the film is another strength of The Godfather. Packed with sharp and profound dialogues, the script takes the audience deep into the world of the complex and intriguing mafia. The internal conflicts within the Corleone family and their struggle to maintain power create a narrative that is so deep and captivating, presenting moral dilemmas that are hard to separate from. The compelling and engaging story keeps the film from ever feeling monotonous, with each scene remaining relevant and significant.

The Godfather also highlights the brilliant direction of Francis Ford Coppola. His cinematographic style perfectly captures the nuances of darkness and tension for this story. The beautiful scene compositions and the use of classical music by Nino Rota make the film highly atmospheric, enhancing its allure.

One thing that makes The Godfather a timeless masterpiece is its skill in presenting complex and sometimes controversial characters. The film delves into the ambivalent nature of humanity and confronts us with intricate moral questions. We witness characters we love and hate, those who are good and evil, all trapped in a web of violence and loyalty.

However, no piece of art is flawless, and The Godfather is no exception. One criticism I can offer is its lengthy duration, although most scenes are valuable, some moments could be trimmed to maintain the story's pace. Additionally, some characters may have benefitted from further development to provide a deeper understanding of their backgrounds.

Overall, The Godfather is a cinematic wonder that has had a profound influence on many films that followed. With brilliant acting, a strong screenplay, and captivating direction, this film is a masterpiece that will be remembered by generations to come. Despite its shortcomings, this is a work that should be appreciated by film enthusiasts and anyone who values the art of filmmaking. The Godfather deserves its place at the top of the list of the greatest films of all time.

10.title: The Godfather is truly extraordinary!
10.content:
I'm struggling to put into words how incredible this movie was. After reading the reviews here, I find it difficult to add anything new, as they've already articulated what makes The Godfather so remarkable. Having watched countless films, both exceptional and lackluster, I can confidently say that The Godfather surpasses them all. Its imagery, intricacies, and memorable scenes have lingered in my mind since I watched it just nine hours ago. The film's craftsmanship and performances elevate it above other remarkable works I've seen, leaving me unable to identify any flaws. While The Godfather may be considered slow-paced and its plot unfolds gradually, these aspects contribute to its elegiac tone and unpredictability. At 18, I was uncertain whether I'd appreciate or comprehend the film, but I found it accessible and can now fully appreciate its status as a masterpiece.

Visually, The Godfather is stunning. Disagreeing with a previous reviewer who criticized the cinematography, I believe it to be one of the film's greatest assets. The cinematography varies from dark and mysterious to vibrant and picturesque, enhancing its overall appeal. Additionally, the meticulously crafted costumes, majestic settings, and immaculate cars further contribute to its visual splendor.

Nina Rota's score is outstanding, leaving a lasting impression with its beauty and haunting melodies. The direction by Francis Ford Coppola and the screenplay, which balances intelligence, thoughtfulness, and dark humor, are equally commendable. While some moments of violence are shocking, they underscore the loyalty and honor within the family depicted in the film.

The performances are exemplary, breathing life into rich and complex characters. Marlon Brando's portrayal of Don Vito is masterful, while Al Pacino's performance, though initially risky, carries the film with finesse. James Caan exudes dignity and loyalty, Diane Keaton captivates with her beauty, and Robert Duvall delivers a nuanced performance.

In conclusion, The Godfather is truly extraordinary, deserving of its status as one of the greatest films ever made. My 15-year-old brother was so enamored with it that he wants to watch it again. While I rate it 10/10, this film transcends such ratings.

The Godfather (1972) is a masterpiece that I recently rewatched for the first time in a long time on Paramount+. The storyline follows an American mafia family with a Godfather who is a direct descendant from Italy. As the father gets older and close to dying and handing down his power within the family he fields a series of asks, favors and political placement requests for power within the underground world.

This movie is directed by Francis Ford Coppola (Apocalypse Now) and stars Marlon Brando (A Streetcar Named Desire), Al Pacino (Scarface), James Caan (Misery), Diane Keaton (Annie Hall), Robert Duvall (Slingblade), Talia Shire (Rocky) and Abe Vigoda (Joe versus the Volcano).

The performances by the entire cast in this movie is outstanding with especially powerful performances by Brando and Pacino and strong supporting performances by Duvall, Caan and Shire. The soundtrack and settings are legendary. This film makes you want to book a trip to Italy immediately. The mafia wedding to start the movie is so well executed and as is the evolution of Pacino's character. The dialogue is brilliantly written and the cast delivers every line with the right level of intensity. The ending a perfect way to end the movie and show the power and struggle of being The Godfather.

Overall this is a cinematic masterpiece that is an absolute must see. I would score this an easy 10/10.

I'm trying to save you money; this is the last film title that you should consider borrowing. Renting Shawshank will cost you five bucks... just plunk down the $25 and own the title. You'll wind up going back to this gem time and time again. This is one of few movies that are truly timeless. And it's entertaining and moving, no matter how many times you view it.

Forget about what others (including myself) might suggest you'll discover in "The Shawshank Redemption;" when you watch it, you'll identify something very personal in your own life with a scene, a character, or a moment in this uncomplicated movie. When you need hope, you'll look for Shawshank. When you want to believe in the will of overcoming even the greatest obstacles, Shawshank will uplift you in ways that you can't find in movies today.

Some liken the film to some kind of spiritual awakening. Of course, some can go to a church or mosque to find enlightenment and Faith in humanity, but most places of worship are open only certain days or times. But when you need affirmation of the lasting bond of friendships that prevail over the most dire circumstances, Shawshank will give it to you. It makes grown men (like me) cry, still. I wonder whether Shawshank was truly meant for viewing in the privacy of the home, because it is a personal experience that really makes you look inward. Nominated for seven, this is the best film that never one a single Oscar.

How ironic that an innocent man winds up being surrounded by the corruption of the legal system. Shawshank itself is similar to the character of Andy Dufresne. Prejudging this classic film, critics couldn't get past the title. The public followed suit, initially dismissing Shawshank, which failed in the box office just like "It's a Wonderful Life" and "Citizen Kane." It could have just whithered away on the store shelves, like Andy Dufresne could have in his own cell. But the characters prevailed, because Andy -- And Shawshank -- stayed true. Now, these movies are right up there as the most popular films of all time.

Anyone who has yet to watch Shawshank may be so jaded of movies, or the film's title, or how a 2-1/2- hour movie set inside the walls of a prison can manage to tap the soul of such a wide range of people. Shawshank has not one explosion. I wonder if it even has a single special effect or digitally- enhanced frame.

But every aspect of Shawshank fit together. The acting from the top to the bit part. The musical score. The editing. The photography. The story, from opening credits to final scene. All involved, including the town of Mansfield, Ohio (where Shawshank was actually filmed) played their roles perfectly. Shawshank is a must- see, must- own title. 10.title: Do Good
10.content:
This film works so well because it takes place in an underworld where we are so embedded that we don't even notice it. Coppola places us smack-dab in the center of what is, admittedly, a society created by criminals for criminals. That's also why it's so welcoming. We're surrounded by its inhabitants - cold-blooded killers who see crime as a 9-to-5 job masquerading as respectable men. And I don't mean men. From the outside, we'll only witness the horrific, disturbing manifestations of their well-thought-out actions.

But it goes deeper than that. It all revolves around the Corleone family, led by Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando). He's the most honest of these men, sitting right on the edge. But for someone like him, who doesn't fully embrace this world, it's not easy. He avoids conflict unless it's absolutely necessary. He's a man defined by moral principles. There's a scene early on where, on the day of his daughter's wedding, one of his associates, Luca Brasi (Lenny Montana), practices the speech he's going to give to the Don when he meets him. The scene with these two is funny and almost adorable. I couldn't help but feel sympathy for both of them, not to mention that I was actually warming up to both of the mobsters. Not to mention that Lenny Montana was a real mob hit-man and was actually nervous as he said this line.

The more I watched, the more I realized how incredibly complex and ruthless this society is and how it has the power to corrupt anyone it comes into contact with. The best example is Corleone's youngest son, Michael (Al Pacino). He returns home for his sister's wedding dressed as a war hero with his longtime girlfriend, Kay Adams (Diane Keaton). At first, he avoids this underworld, but necessity, first-hand exposure, and the sheer devilish allure of it draw him in. As we progress through the film, the transformation is dramatic, and every outsider who comes close to him is tainted. One way or another. If they survive, they are drawn in, as are we as viewers.

Inside, Coppola presents the family in its entirety to us with a boldly personal approach, and we witness every discussion, every methodically calculated choice. Crime is committed simply because it is the nature of their business, and we are put in a chair alongside them, so we relate easily. To us, they are the good guys, the rival family the bad guys. The greatest achievement this film has managed to pull off is separating the good guys and the bad guys in a world full of bad guys.

This is a film of unparalleled subtlety. No other film holds its own so well. No other film is done with such precision, attention, and completeness. There are so many layers that I probably missed and may never notice. But I felt them. What director Francis Ford Coppola and his partner in crime (poor choice of words, sorry) Mario Puzo did is nothing less than a timeless reference movie whose impact is based not on reinventing the wheel, but on making it perfectly optimal.

Most masterpieces are remembered for their historical contributions. "Citizen Kane" brought the biggest step forward in the art form, the same things "Gone with the Wind" or "2001: A Space Odyssey" did. "The Godfather" is one of the few films that will be remembered because they are so good, and I can't possibly imagine a greater achievement than that.

10.title: Film after book is really something else 1/2
10.content:
If I remember it correctly, this is my 3rd or 4th time watching this movie. First time was in my university years or earlier, I still remember how I was overwhelmed by the plethora of faces, names, relationships and the rapid succession of different scenes in the movie, that I fell asleep within 15 minutes. Later when I grew more, I finished watching the movie and began to really like it. Still I must say there was a lot that I failed to understand in the movie.

Now, ten or more years have passed since my first watch, I finally found time to finish reading the classic book by Mario Puzo, and driven by the lingering excitement, watched watching this movie again. I must say, with knowledge from the book, the film came alive for me on so many levels. Not only can I effortlessly remember, or rather, actively seeking the names and characters I enjoy so much, I could link the stories in so smoothly that I felt a sense of achievement in myself. Not to mention the subtle emotions, internal monologues and more that a film may find hard to display.

On the other hand, I also enjoyed thoroughly in finding the differences between the original book and film adaptation. I must say while there are a lot of things left out and dropped (which is quite a pity for me, while inevitably), the exceptional performance, lighting, adaptation and more really made up for it, and enabled an original fan like me to see through other angles of this story. It's like to read the book a second time.

This being said, I will write down some of the more obvious differences that I have observed, just for my future reference should I decide to read the book again or watch this masterpiece with my family or friends.

1. In the book, Bonasera the undertaker was the last one to be summoned for an audience with the Don, for the Don may want to keep him waiting and hanging. In the movie, he seems to be the first, before the baker even. Also just personally, I imagined Bonasera to be more "bony" than in movie, for some reason.

2. Barzini, not mentioned in the book until later, shows up in the movie to attend the wedding, and actually orders his man to destroy some cameras when shot a picture.

3. Paulie seems to be lazier in movie, for Clemenza needs to yell at him to bring him more wine after a hot dance!

4. In the book, Sonny's wife Sanda is said to be "coarse, strongly built with great breasts" who seemed to be blessingly carefree of Sonny's screwing around (until later). In the movie, she seems to be a slender, rightfully jealous as delicate American wife who warns Sonny to "watch yourself".

5. Poor boy Nino Valenti is dropped in film, so is doctor Jules Segal, thus a lot of stories and interactions among these two and Johnny Fontane, Lucy Mancini are lost. Such a pity.

6. Fredo is bold enough to come up and kiss Kay Adams in the wedding before Mike in movie.

7. In book, Sonny is visibly nervous when Hagen knocks on the door and stops banging Lucy immediately. In movie he asks for "one minute" more his fun. Movie really pictures Sonny as a more primitive birdbrain than book, without emphasizing his tactical genius in wars.

8. Movie adds the scene of family picture shot, twice. The first time the Don refused to take the picture without Mike. A good touch. Another scene added is the Don dancing with daughter.

9. In movie, Tom Hagen seems to be able to see Jack Woltz easily while he's working in studio? Not very realistic for me. Also, it's a pity that Woltz's mother & daughter "playmates" are dropped.

10. Luca Brasi seems to be less deft and alert in movie when he's murdered, given all the bright lighting and his lack of evading the attacks.

11. In movie, the Don didn't call out Fredo's name when shot. Fredo actually drew his gun, but fumbled and dropped it. The latter one is a good touch.

12. In book, it's Michael who doesn't understand the meaning of Luca's vest sent with a fish. This makes better sense than Sonny asking "what the hell is this" in movie.

13. Does Rocco Lampone ever shows his face in movie? He certainly doesn't have a place in the closing credit. This being said, he's name is called out by Paulie Gatto in the car where he's about to be killed. And it could be argued that just as in the book, he's the one to kill Don Tattaglia later in the baptism scene.

14. The last meeting of Mikey and Kay before Mike's exile is in their room eating dinner in a silent manner, not as intimate as having a quickie as in book, if you ask me.

15. Enzo, the baker's son-in-law, is used to pretend to be a gunman by Mike outside the hospital in movie. In book, they just stand their together. A win for the movie.

16. Captain Mark McCluskey is portrayed as an old guy in the movie, while I used to imagine him to be around 40-50 years old. His dirty talks after a random lawyer (replaced by Tom in movie) appeared to Michael is dropped in movie.

17. Mike actually get pissed by Sonny's laugh at his proposition to kill the cop and Turk. He has an impassive face in movie.

18. In the Italian restaurant scene, Sollozzo seems to be less alert than in the book, by sitting with his back facing the toilet (well yes he at least looked back when Mikey came out), and didn't start to dodge when Mike pulled the gun.

19. Mike is a bit clumsy when "tossing" the gun in movie (yes his arm actually flung up in the air), making a "thud" sound when gun hitting the floor. In book, the gun should be slipping to the floor and no one could catch a sound.

20. In movie, Fredo is sent to LA under Sonny's order. A win for Sonny I guess. Also the Don, when sent home from hospital, asked about "where is Michael" in his feeble voice, and became visibly frustrated and sad when he got the news. A good adaptaion.

21. In Sicily, Dr. Taza is dropped, gone together the scene where he attends to a very sick Mike after the bomb. Old lady Filomena is dropped too, whose main purpose in book was to give the story of how scary and horrible a man Luca Brasi had been.

22. Don Tommasino in Sicily is much fatter and tenderer than I thought him to be. Also for some reason, he's depicted to be sitting in a wheelchair in the wedding procession. Something I don't quite understand.

23. I wished to see the awesome tattoo shepherd Fabrizzio gets on his chest, not something shown in movie.

24. Fabrizzio seems to be very exciting with American movies, cars and everything in movie. A good foreshadowing for his moving to America, though this is something not shown in movie.

25. The gang meets Apollonia and the girls while walking. In book, the gang was dozing off under some shadows of orange groves.

26. Appolonia is so innocently beautiful! This being said, while I'm not familiar with how Italian girls look, I guess she seem a bit more mature than a "16-year-old"?

27. In movie when talking to Apollonia's father, Mike is speaking English using Fabrizzio as a translator, instead of speaking Italian/Sicilian, something I don't quite understand.

28. Appolonia "fell" a bit when walking on a flat dirt road, not up the hill where she lives. Guess she really likes Mikey too!

29. Back to Long Island, when handing the letter, Kay doesn't get a chance meeting with Mama Corleone. Sad. I always love their chemistry.

30. Mama Corleone speaks with fluent American English when taking the call from a desperate Connie. Maybe the movie doesn't need her to be a poor English speaker with a heavy Italian accent? Also, she looks much younger and plump to me, without all the "croan-ness".

31. On this note, all her dropped interactions with Kay is something to be missed, including her cooking and prepping coffee for Kay after she returns the Mall after Mike returns, and her persuading Kay to convert to Catholics.

32. Sonny drives out of the Mall to beat the shit out of Carlo actually takes place in broad daylight instead of 4am in the morning. And he's gunned down by...almost 10 people is a bit over the top. More so when he could open the door and walk a bit, after getting destroyed with so many Thompsons...

33. The Don is much more visibly sad when looking at Sonny's corpse before Bonesera. In book, "for one fraction of a second the Don put out his hand to support himself against Bonasera's body". This is so much so when Tom first breaks this news to him, while in book, "Don Corleone blinked. For just the fraction of a second the wall of his will disintegrated and the draining of his physical strength was plain on his face. Then he recovered." I must say I like both the movie and the book here. By the way, the author really likes to use "for a fraction of a second"!

34. Also, when hearing the news from Tom, the Don really recovered quick to the point that he could give out orders like "I want no inquiries made, I want no acts of vengeance...". In the book, it's only after the capos arrive and some discussion that the Don make the orders.

35. Back to Mike. While his broken jaw/face is not as twisted as I thought, nice touch to the detail to give him a handkerchief to wipe his nose!

36. The movies is more convincing to make Mike realize there's a bomb in car when he sees Fabrizzio hurriedly leave the gate. In the book it's out of some mysterious instinct that a reader may find hard to understand. Also, the remains of Alfa Romeo looks more than just "its four wheels and the steel shafts which held them together". Guess this is to show the remains of poor Appolonia's dress in the car.

10.title: The Godfather
10.content:
The Godfather is a 1972 Ameerican crime film, directed by Francis Ford Coppola and produced by Albert S. Ruddy with a screenplay by Mario Puzo and Coppola. Starring Marlon Brando and Al Pacino as the leaders of a New York crime family, the story covers the years 1945-1955, focusing on the transformation of Michael Corleone who later became a ruthless Mafia boss with Vito as the head of the Corleone Family.

Based on Puzo's best-selling novel of the same name, The Godfather is generally considered one of the greatest films in world cinema, and also one of the most influential films, especially in the Gangster genre. Second only to Citizen Kane being torn down by the American Film Institute in 2007, the film was selected for preservation in the United States National Film Registry in 1990.

The film is the highest-grossing film ever made, and remained the box office leader in 1972. The film won three Oscars that year: Best Picture, Best Actor and Best Adapted Screenplay for Puzo and Coppola. Nominations in seven other categories include Pacino, James Caan, and Robert Duvall for Best Supporting Actor and Coppola for Best Director. The success of this film gave birth to two follow-up films: The Godfather Part II in 1974, and The Godfather Part III in 1990.

10.title: A Timeless Masterpiece!
10.content:
Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather is not just a film; it is an experience. The moment the film begins, you're drawn into a world so rich, so complex, and so beautifully crafted that it's impossible to look away. The story of the Corleone family, their rise to power, and the loyalty, betrayal, and sacrifice that come with it, is told with such depth and precision that it feels as if you're witnessing history unfold. Every element of this film-its acting, direction, writing, and music-works in perfect harmony to create a cinematic masterpiece.

Marlon Brando's portrayal of Vito Corleone is legendary. He doesn't just play the character; he becomes him. With every deliberate movement, every whisper of dialogue, Brando paints a picture of a man who is both feared and respected, whose kindness and ruthlessness coexist in a delicate balance. The now-iconic "I'm gonna make him an offer he can't refuse" line? It's a moment that will send chills down your spine every single time you hear it, because Brando delivers it with such authority and depth. His performance is a perfect blend of subtlety and power, elevating the film to new heights.

And then there's Al Pacino, who, in the role of Michael Corleone, goes through a transformation that is nothing short of extraordinary. When we first meet Michael, he is an outsider to the family business, a man of honor who wants to distance himself from the violence and corruption that surround him. But as the story unfolds, we watch Michael's descent into the dark world of organized crime, and Pacino's performance is nothing short of mesmerizing. His ability to convey Michael's internal conflict, his struggle between loyalty to his family and his desire for a different life, is haunting and unforgettable. By the film's conclusion, Pacino has crafted one of the most compelling character arcs in film history.

The screenplay, written by Mario Puzo and Coppola, is pure genius. It doesn't rush to tell its story; it allows the audience to immerse themselves in the lives of these complex characters. The power struggles, family dynamics, and personal tragedies unfold slowly and methodically, creating a tension that never lets up. The Godfather isn't just a story about crime; it's a poignant commentary on power, loyalty, and the human condition. The family's devotion to each other is both touching and tragic, and as the film progresses, we realize that the Corleones are a family bound by blood, but also by the choices they've made and the lives they've taken.

Coppola's direction is nothing short of masterful. He understands the nuances of the script and brings it to life with incredible attention to detail. Every frame feels purposeful, every scene meticulously composed. The lighting, especially, is a crucial part of the film's atmosphere. The use of shadows creates a sense of mystery, danger, and moral ambiguity. And the pacing? Perfect. The film is long, but it never drags. You're never bored because there's always something captivating happening on screen, whether it's a tense conversation, a violent confrontation, or a quiet moment of reflection.

The music by Nino Rota is the perfect complement to the film's tone. The hauntingly beautiful score sticks with you long after the film ends, evoking feelings of nostalgia, melancholy, and, at times, dread. The music doesn't just accompany the story-it becomes a part of it, deepening the emotional impact of every scene.

In the end, The Godfather is more than just a film. It's an exploration of family, power, loyalty, and the choices that define us. It is a story that resonates on a universal level, one that continues to be relevant and impactful even decades after its release. Every time I watch it, I discover something new, something I missed before, and that's what makes it so special. The Godfather is not just a classic; it's a timeless work of art that will remain at the top of the cinematic world for generations to come.

10.title: Best movie ever!
10.content:
What more is there to say that hasn't been said? This is hands down my favorite movie of all time? "The Godfather" stands as an enduring testament to the power of storytelling and filmmaking. Widely regarded as the greatest movie of all time, this cinematic gem has transcended its genre, leaving an indelible mark on both the film industry and popular culture. Several elements contribute to its status as the pinnacle of cinematic achievement.

At the heart of the movie is a compelling narrative that unfolds with meticulous precision. Mario Puzo's source material, combined with Coppola's adept screenplay, weaves a tale of power, family, and betrayal. The film effortlessly navigates the complex dynamics of the Corleone crime family, delving into the intricacies of their relationships, both familial and criminal. The narrative unfolds in a series of interconnected events, creating a rich tapestry that captivates the audience from start to finish. Central to the film's success are its iconic characters, brought to life by an ensemble cast delivering career-defining performances. Marlon Brando's portrayal of Vito Corleone is nothing short of legendary, a nuanced and powerful performance that earned him an Academy Award. Al Pacino's transformation from a reluctant outsider to a ruthless leader as Michael Corleone is a masterclass in character development. The ensemble, including James Caan, Robert Duvall, and John Cazale, complements the leads, creating a memorable cast of characters that have become archetypes in cinematic history. The women in the film are very under-appreciated and deserve more recognition, including Simonetta Stefani as Apollonia, Diane Keaton as Kay-Addams Corleone, and Talia Shire as Connie Corleone. Coppola's directorial brilliance is evident in every frame of the film. The film's cinematography, led by Gordon Willis, is a visual symphony, employing a rich color palette and innovative techniques to evoke the mood and tone of each scene.
