8.content: It captures a dark world,at it's darkest and most violent,yet there are moments of beauty sprinkled throughout.This is what I enjoyed about The Godfather.I'm not a huge fan of mafia themed films,but I will give this film credit for presenting it with such realism.We get lost in it's realities and we forget often throughout the film that it is,in fact just a movie and that it is all play acting.I was wowed by how well casted it was and how well suited for their characters each actor was,in particular Marlon Brando.For all of it's dark theme and violent content,The Godfather still manages to come out looking like a true masterpiece.

8.title: Watch it twice!
8.content:
I wasn't too impressed by this film the first time I saw it. However, it got better the more I saw it. A movie like this would be impossible to make today. Francis Ford Coppola is a marvelous director and loves his characters in order to get authentic performances out of them.

The violence is brutal, the script is superb, and the soundtrack is incredible. Everyone involved should be proud at what they accomplished. I never read the book but fans say it's a faithful adaptation. Goodfellas is a mobster film I like slightly more but The Godfather is still a cinematic achievement. I know some people are going to get on my case for not calling it the best movie ever made in the history of mankind, but I'm not denying that it's a good movie.

Just watch it more than once to enjoy it for what it is and you'll love it like I did!

8.title: masterpiece
8.content: This movie is strong, good script, great casting, excellent acting, and over the top directing. It is hard to fine a movie done this well, it is 29 years old and has aged well. Even if the viewer does not like mafia type of movies, he or she will watch the entire film, the audiences is glued to what will happen next as the film progresses. Its about, family, loyalty, greed, relationships, and real life. This is a great mix, and the artistic style make the film memorable.audiences is glued to what will happen next as the film progresses. Its about, family, loyalty, greed, relationships, and real life. This is a great mix, and the artistic style make the film memorable.

8.title: Sometimes it's too slow for my taste, but after all an enchaining story, with great characters.
8.content: First of all, it's been a while since I decided to watch The Godfather, but somehow I've never had enough will power to do so. I heard people saying it's the greatest movie of all time, but I was still being skeptical about this statement, as I couldn't imagine a movie with such long play time grabbing your attention all over it. When it started playing I could sense the outstanding feeling of the early 50's USA. It just felt natural to be part of this world, as we were born to it. The plot is not to be detailed, as it's one of the most famous movies, but I can assure everyone, this is the strongest part of the film. Of course there are some action scenes where bad people shoot with guns, there are some romantic scenes where beautiful woman make love with handsome man, but all of these give the essential of the Godfather. We learn the rules of this world, without directly being taught each of them. We become the part of the family, and we suffer or win, as the Corleones do. We start to worry about the characters, that feel alive and feel realistic. Our first, probably negative impression are getting overwrite by the deeper, and more considered emotions, which are more likely to be positive. We understand that some things have to be done, no matter what the morals say. Yes, we can live the life of the Corleones, and that's a thing not every movie can provide. The Godfather is not the best movie of all time, not for me at least. But it surely worth watching, not just because it's a legend, but for why it has become a legend.

8.title: Brilliant, but not the 'greatest movie ever made'
8.content:
The Godfather has been timelessly voted the best movie ever, over and over and over again, but its not!!!! However, do not let this opinionated view fool you, it is a fantastic film with nothing wrong with it. This films ranks up with the other most over rated films in existence, such as Star wars: a new hope and Apocalypse now.

The films starts off at a wedding, the daughter of the infamous 'Godfather' is getting married, and we soon find out that on this day of all days, no father can refuse a request. More subplots follow and some interesting dialog is put forward, until the Godfather is gunned down by a rival family. However, he does not die but is in injured, along the way his son dies, and the son of the man who tried to kill him dies. The Godfathers youngest son Michael has to flee the country as he is the one who killed the rival family members son, The godfather is upset as he wanted Michael to be the legitimate member of the family. The plot goes by and Michael returns, and along with the Godfather they kill all the head members of the leading rival families. This is not the best plot summary in the world but it will do.

The film is flawless, as many people constantly state. The acting is great, although Brando should not have won a best actor Oscar? All the other 3 should not have even been nominated for best supporting actors and actresses. But besides this, the give great performances. The script is where most of the talents truly lie, a brilliant story of the Mafia and how it operates, filled with loyalty and betrail this is a film which takes you on an intense and emotional ride. But this film is very very boring in some places, for instance when Michael is hiding out in Italy. Now im no shallow person who has to have action and explosions in movies to feel satisfied, but for a film to be crowned the greatest ever you have to love every bit of the film completely, and everyone will admit there are very boring bits in this. However still a great film. In my opinion, if you really want to a crown a film the best ever, you should look to titles such as Terminator 2, Shawshank Redemption, Master and Commander: The far side of the world, Lord of the rings trilogy

8.title: best film
8.content:
We know from Gay Talese's book Honor Thy Father that being a professional mobster isn't all sunshine and roses. More often, it's the boredom of stuffy rooms and a bad diet of carry-out food, punctuated by brief, terrible bursts of violence. This is exactly the feel of "The Godfather," which brushes aside the flashy glamour of the traditional gangster picture and gives us what's left: fierce tribal loyalties, deadly little neighborhood quarrels in Brooklyn, and a form of vengeance to match every affront.

Advertisement

The remarkable thing about Mario Puzo's novel was the way it seemed to be told from the inside out; he didn't give us a world of international intrigue, but a private club as constricted as the seventh grade. Everybody knew everybody else and had a pretty shrewd hunch what they were up to.

The movie (based on a script labored over for some time by Puzo and then finally given form, I suspect, by director Francis Ford Coppola) gets the same feel. We tend to identify with Don Corleone's family not because we dig gang wars, but because we have been with them from the beginning, watching them wait for battle while sitting at the kitchen table and eating chow mein out of paper cartons.

"The Godfather" himself is not even the central character in the drama. That position goes to the youngest, brightest son, Michael, who understands the nature of his father's position while revising his old-fashioned ways. The Godfather's role in the family enterprise is described by his name; he stands outside the next generation which will carry on and, hopefully, angle the family into legitimate enterprises.

8.title: A great film, though not as great as some will say.
8.content:
The Godfather is a story surrounding an organized crime family named Corleone in the 1940's. The patriarch, Don Vito Corleone, his loyal son Sonny, his daughter Connie who marries the abusive Carlo Rizzi, and his legitimate son Michael who is not involved in the family business. When Michael returns home from the war and Don Corleone is nearly killed by a rival gang, he slowly finds himself being sucked into the life. Though many people will say The Godfather is the greatest movie of all time, it's not. To tell you the truth, it's not an exciting movie at all. It's not action packed, and not a whole lot happens in its 3 hour running time. However, it is a brilliantly made film with some amazing acting, and portrays the most realistic view of the mafia in film history.

Let's start off with the acting. Al Pacino who is now recognized as one of the best actors of all time got his start as Michael Corleone in this film. The movie mainly focuses on his getting sucked into the family business. Al Pacino plays the role brilliantly showing both his tempted side and his reluctant side. All of the supporting actors in this film are awesome. There are really solid performances by James Caan as Sonny who has the coolest scene in the film, and Robert Duvall as Tom. Of course, nothing bad can be said about the late Marlon Brando's performance as Don Vito Corleone. This is Brando's most famous role and for good reason. His genius portrayal will go down in history as one of the greatest acting jobs of all time.

The realism of the film is what also makes it good. This is the most realistic view of the mafia you will ever see on film. Most mafia films portray the action side of the story with all the hit men and explosions and gunfights. The Godfather doesn't show a lot of that. It focuses mainly on the business side of things. It shows how serious mobsters really are about their jobs.

So, even though The Godfather isn't the greatest film of all time, it's one of the best made.

8.5/10

8.title: The Sicilian Way doesn't work in the Anglo-Saxon world
8.content:
If you lived in Sicily over the last 3,000 years you'd be pretty used to death and devastation by now. Sicily is bang smack in the middle of three prominent pre-Christian empires: the Greek post-Alexander Hellenistic empire, the Roman Empire and the Carthagian-Lavantine Empire. All three of them fought tooth and nail for 3 centuries to control Sicily. And I haven't mentioned yet the tyrants who used to rule Sicilian cities such as Syracuse, for whom the Greek engineer Archimedes worked. Then came the bully-boy, Normans, the Hapsburg Empire, Napoleon, Mussolini, the Nazis...oh where does it end?

In other words, dying, or threatening others with death, is just something else to do on a Sunday afternoon in Sicily. The Sicilians also learnt how to barter with their masters of the day, and how to subjugate their own.

Transfer all of this to a quiet neighbourhood of New York City, and it's like trusting King Kong into the city to clean the windows of the Empire State Building.

The Godfather, adapted from Mario Puzo's novel, shows how capable the Sicilian Mafia are at subduing the authorities to run their own profiteering rackets. But what's interesting is how after the Godfather was shown, how the authorities decided they had had enough of being manipulated by Sicilians. It wasn't long before they put every effort into suppressing these usurpers. The US authorities regained the role the Greeks, Romans and Carthagians had once held.

Sicilian management is impressive, but not as impressive as good old Dutch-Anglo-Saxon mastery of all things profitable.

A point of interest, the decapitation of the horse-head scene in this movie has its foundation in Roman Chariot racing on The Field Of Mars. One of the winning horses would be sacrificed, it's blood mixed with the bodies of the unborn children and its head nailed to the door of the Forum.

"The Godfather" has become a classic in the 28 years since its release. It's definitely a great movie, that hasn't lost any of it's brilliance. The problems of Don Vito's life are still strong today, especially the issue of drugs.

8.content:
A very good film. Good story and good acting and directing.

But it's not the best Gangster film ever made.

That award goes to the Director's cut of Once Upon a Time in America. It's a film that has much more depth to it than does The Godfather.

The Godfather is an entertaining evening, but it doesn't move you. You don't really care about any of the characters---they are all just psychopaths with no depth to them. We hardly even known Vito Corleone's wife, for example.

Terrific story, but nothing with much depth. They are gangsters and nothing more. It's a move about 'business" but not about what life would have really been like for them. People die, ho hum. Do we really miss any of them as people? For your sake, I hope not.

8.title: Well made and well acted but ultimately slow paced and pretty boring.
8.content: After seeing this movie numerous times I have to say that overall I find it highly overrated. It is definately well crafted and the acting is superb. However the pacing is dreadfully slow at times and while I think overall the acting is strong it does get a little overblown at times. Definately one of the best movies in its genre, unfortunately imho its not a genre with many good films.

8.title: Just a Bit Too Long, but Still Pretty Great
8.content:
The Godfather has great scenes, classic characters, classic dialogue, and an amusing look into the Italian mafioso, but it's just a tad bit too long to be perfect, in my opinion as a new viewer. There were many scenes that were riveting and performances that were, at times, mesmerizing, but I just feel like it is a little overrated.

It deserves its due credit, no doubt, for without it, so many great movies and tv shows inspired by it would have never been made, and the ground it therefore broke will always hold its place as one of the greatest movies ever made. Some scenes were just too drawn out, lengthened, or long-winded, and it can therefore become a little bit of a chore to watch and enjoy in one sitting, as good as it can be at certain points.

I can see how when this came out in 1974, it was so popular and how it held up throughout the years to be considered one of the best movies ever made, but in my experience in watching other movies since then of this genre, I can list at least 5 I enjoy at least just as much if not more. Obviously, those films have been inspired by the Godfather so without it they wouldn't likely exist in the fashion that they do, but they are still better paced, more suspenseful at times, and just more entertaining overall.

This doesn't mean that the Godfather isn't a classic and one of the best, but it is a matter of taste, and the Godfather still remains a movie I have to really be in the mood for to sit through. Certain scenes, or parts, of this epic hold up much more than others, while other parts and scenes can feel like a slog to sit through.

8/10

8.title: Good, but this is not what mob life is like
8.content: I know because I knew a mob guy. This is Hollywood's glorification of the worst possible life to choose. Phenomenal acting, but the life of a mob guy is violent and depraved (and often broke). The most realistic mob movie I have ever seen is Donnie Brasco. This is what mob life is really like. Mob life is about a million miles from being romantic. Carlito's Way is another realistic (more or less) look at street crime life. you watch this movie for the phenomenal acting, not for realism in any way. Hollywood loves to capitalize off stories of gangsters, glorify it up a bit, and package it as if it were real. What's real is busting your hump, not making enough in a month so you have to sell dope, and wondering if there is a gun at your head every second of the day. to be honest, I'd rather sell staplers.

The tale of a crime organization in the 1940s that go into a struggle for power when the leader is shot and hospitalized in a conspiracy, though continuously tended by his trusted sons, played by some of the now famous actors ever, including James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Al Pacino. Coppola's best work ever, and one of the greatest films ever made!

8.title: Excellent Execution.
8.content:
It's a beautifully made movie. Not just because of the subtle direction by Francis Coppola but because of the production design (Dean Tavoularis) and photography (Gordon Willis). Everything seems to lend itself to the impact of the story, which describes the replacement of Marlon Brando's Mafia chief by his youngest son, Al Pacino. Make up is expertly handled. Pacino's broken cheek is properly swollen and blue and fades gradually, providing the viewer with a kind of cinematic clock telling the passage of time. Nino Rota's score is tops. During the baptism scene, which takes place in a church, the organ hums an apt courtly tune. Then, as the film cross cuts between ritualized religion and ritualized homicide, the organ insensibly becomes darker and more ominous.

These departments seldom get enough credit -- except recently in CGI extravaganza's. The more nuanced touches in furnishings, wardrobe, shadows and the like generally go unrewarded by the public. But this film, and a few others like it ("Shane", "Verdict") wouldn't be what they are if they'd been clumsily handled.

Brando has given maybe four nearly perfect performances and this is one of them. To appreciate it we have to skip over all his failed attempts to extend his range, the dancing bookmaker, the comic Oriental sidekick. The Don Corleone we see doesn't radiate power so much as fatigue. Al Pacino is transformed from a smiling lad, happy to be home from the war, to a dispassionate kingpin of crime at the end, a bit too abruptly. Sterling Hayden, as the corrupt Irish cop, has invested this much in a role only once before, in "Dr. Strangelove." Example: After smashing Pacino's face with one blow of his oversized fist, Hayden turns away, winces with self control and pounds his fist into the night-time air.

It's hard to imagine how Coppola could have improved on his direction of this tragic tale. With the exception of the violent scenes, of which there are many, maybe too many, the film's texture is smooth and understated. Example: A baker shows up at the hospital just before some would-be assassins arrive and Pacino talks this innocent man into posing as a gunman. Not a word from the baker. He does what he's told. And when it's safe, he tries to light a cigarette but his hands are shaking so badly that Pacino has to light it for him.

The women don't have much to do. Diane Keaton as the Shiksa is puzzled but hopeful. Talia Shire as the abused wife is hysterical. Mamma Corleone is a revered background figure who rarely shows up.

That's the good stuff -- and it's very good indeed.

The bad stuff, I'm not sure about. The Corleone family, like the other five families in New York, are making a fortune. That's evident from their digs, their cars, their raw silk suits. But what business are they in? That's one of the things Keaton is curious about. The businesses are only alluded to twice -- " the gambling, the liquor, even the women." Well, what's so bad about that? Who gives a damn about illegal gambling, smuggled liquor, or escort services? Nobody. Drugs are brought in towards the end, but only dealt with discretely. We never sell it around schools, it must be strictly controlled, and let the darkies up in Harlem have it and "kill their souls." The words "extortion," "protection racket," and "Mafia" are never used.

This is a pretty rotten business they're in. And if Marlon Brando' Don was a kind of community organizer, Al Pacino's Don is a ruthless hypocrite. In fact, he's a lying, murdering, thief. While he is solemnly taking his oath as godfather to his nephew, his minions are out in the streets slaughtering rivals wholesale -- and in the most graphic way.

"Never ask me about my business," he tells his wife. And one hopes she never does, unless she wants to wind up "sleeping with the fishes."

8.title: Not the best ever
8.content: I personally believe that this movie is overrated. I don't really even believe it is the best work from a Coppola (I personally believe "Apocalypse Now" and "Lost in Translation" are much better movies), but it still is entertaining to watch. It has notable performances by Marlon Brando and Al Pacino (perhaps the only Pacino performance other than "Glengarry Glen Ross" where he doesn't scream his eyes out), and the film also has a very nice screenplay, but the movie isn't as entertaining or extraordinary as other frontrunners like "Casablanca" or "Lawrence of Arabia". Maybe because this movie has been marred by so many rip-offs or clones, that the magic of the film has disappeared. The film just no longer feels ageless, and that's too bad.

8.title: Good, but not that good
8.content:
Let me start by saying that I didn't particularly enjoy the Godfather. I found the film too slow paced, and James Caan was extremely irritable. Vito took FOREVER to recover, and when he did he choked it not long later.

Saying that, I respect the film and Coppola on the effort and technical prowess on show. Al Pacino is brilliant, if a little predictable, while Robert Duvall steals the spotlight if you ask me, with a truly masterful performance.

The final scene will always be remembered, and for good reason, its artistically genius, but I won'y give it away.

This film isn't for everyone, so don't worry if you think you oughta enjoy it just because it's ranked number 1 in the top 250. Just remember that films are always about opinion, and there can never be justifiable official "Greatest Movie", so if you don't like it fine, don't let other people hound you down just because they insist that it's the perfect film, because as far as I'm concerned, there can never be a perfect film.

As Peter Griffin once said, "It insists upon itself Louis".

8.title: Godfather, the best movie of all times? Gimme a break...
8.content:
Godfather the best movie of all times, and the only movie worth a 9/10, and Godfather 2 the third best movie?? Come on..., the Godfather series has its moments and especially the first one is not a bad movie at all. But, IMHO, almost all the other major movies about Mafia (especially "Goodfellas" & "Once Upon a Time in America") are, more interesting and better art too than the bombastic Godfather series. I find even Brando's acting in these movies below his normal standards.

And let me tell you why many people like these mafia movies so much: it's just because many people secretly in their heart admire and envy the "wild & free" life style of the gangsters. Just the same reason why Bonnie & Clyde etc. are so popular. Or youngsters love to read the Nicky Cruz biography "Run, baby, run" because they find the violent & brutal life of the young gangsters exciting and fascinating, blindly ignoring the fact that the author's message is totally against that. Sadly, it is often the same with movies. You think Quentin Tarantino is so popular among the masses because of his artistic merits? You think wrong.

8.content: I personally believe that Godfater is one the most boring but "Famous" movies of all time.The moment anybody hears the word GODFATHER they ""want"" to believe that this is the best movie of all but in the real sense it is far from being great.People tell that AL Pacino got known by this movie but all he ever did was keep his mouth shut except for a few scenes unlike his other movies like Scarface,Heat,Devil's Advocate,Dog Day Afternoon etc.Even the ""great Marlon Brando"" did not have much role in it.The entire movie is filled with conversation and nothing else.If there was A man in this entire planet who never saw or even heard anything about any movie,and you show him "The Godfather",I bet that he would probably go to sleep within the first 10 minutes.We the people of todays generation are made to believe that this is the best movie of all time by the media and other people.Honestly the only reason i saw this movie was to find out what the hell was there in it that is receiving so much appreciation.Guys who have not seen this movie might also be thinking the same that this movie is the best bit in reality,it is not.This movie is a very long piece of ****

8.title: Classic movie
8.content: This classic has lasted the test of time. Always great to watch.

8.title: A Movie You Can't Refuse
8.content:
Though I don't think The Godfather should be the #2 movie on the top 250, I understand it's importance to the industry. I understand that there's more depth in The Godfather than most movies of the time. I don't know, I keep a pretty open mind to movies and the different eras they were made in. 1970-1980 just isn't a popular decade for me. So far, The Godfather series is probably the best thing to come out of this era (or at least the first two). It's a pretty big hit. I loved it. I just didn't love it as much as the movie masses do even to this day. The story is rich, and Vito Corleone is easily one of my favorite characters of all time now. The death scenes are brutal and hard-hitting. The director didn't waste a single gunshot or strangulation for the sake of just doing it. There's a method to the madness of The Godfather, and I guess thats' why it hits people so hard. They story is built up in a way to where the killing of a character hits just as hard as your favorite character leaving the cast of your favorite sitcom.

The scene in the garden with Don Vito and his grandson is by far my favorite. Out of all the ways I'd expect it to happen, It took me by surprise. It was a very sweet and heartfelt scene, and the character was too worthy of it. I would've been angry if Vito ended as a victim, and not the legend... the Godfather.

Check this movie out. There's a good reason why it's such an important movie to the industry. Other than that - it's just a fantastic piece of cinema, and touches on a few topics we can all relate to: Honor, Nobility, and Family.

8.title: A proper mafia film
8.content: This movie is MORE deserving of the spot held by Shawshank on this site as the best movie of all time. The film was rather concise, leaving the viewer with a desire for more. The main character, bizarre voice aside, was a character that is easy to get attached too, both in part to the well written script, and on point acting. A classic movie everyone should see. I am glad to have a movie in the top 5 that is an example of nearly unanimous support.

8.title: great
8.content: Best out of all 3, great to watch with friends or family or with your pet. like your cat or maybe your dog spot. well I dont know if his name is really spot or just a nickname. what was it we were talking about? oh yeah, the godfather, great movie.

8.title: The whole
8.content:
This is a great film in that it is expertly choreographed with expert cinematography.

Ganster films are not my cup of tea but if you have to watch one it should be this one.

That being said, if you don't watch to the end then you don't get the full story/film.

It is long and can be arduous but you have to stick with all of it. It is a detailed nuanced story.

Again, not my bag, but masterfully made and acted.

8.title: Superb
8.content:
There is very little that I can add to the reviews on here, that have explained what is so wonderful about The Godfather so well. I have seen many amazing movies, as well as some clunkers, but The Godfather was beyond amazing. There are so many images, details and scenes that I seriously cannot get out of my head since watching it for the first time just nine hours ago. The Godfather is so incredibly well-made and acted that it stands out among the rest of those other amazing films I've seen, so much so I couldn't think of a single flaw, and I am struggling to think of a good enough reason to why I didn't see this film before now.

True, The Godfather is a little slow-moving and the plot takes a while to unfold, but neither of these are flaws as such. The slow pacing added to the elegiac quality The Godfather has, and as for the plot what is special about this plot is that it is very unpredictable because you have next to no idea where it is next going to take you. Being 18, I was worried whether I was old enough to appreciate this film or even understand it, but luckily I understood it perfectly, and I can well and truly appreciate it for the masterpiece it is considered to be.

The Godfather for one thing looks stunning. I strongly disagree with the previous reviewer who said the cinematography was horrid, for me the cinematography was one of the best assets of the film. In some scenes you have cinematography and lighting that is quite dark and mysterious, and then in scenes such as the wedding it is evergreen, autumnal and very picturesque. It is not just the cinematography that makes The Godfather look stunning, the costumes are beautifully tailored, the houses are gorgeous and majestic to look at and even the cars were immaculate.

Then there is the score by Nina Rota. One word, outstanding! I have heard many wonderful scores in my lifetime, but after hearing this score few stick in the memory as much as the score for The Godfather. This score is both beautiful as seen with the main theme, and haunting in the way it sticks in your head after watching the film itself. Other outstanding assets are the masterly direction from Francis Ford Coppola, and the brilliantly written screenplay that is intelligent, thought-provoking and darkly humorous. As for the violence, some of it is shocking and intense especially in the climax which was enough to almost make your heart either beat twice as fast or stop, and I almost covered my eyes when the producer found the horse's head in his bed, but underneath that this family is somewhat loyal and honourable come to think of it.

8.title: Light and darkness
8.content:
Besides being one of the first films to sympathize with the bad guys, "The Godfather" is not particularly mind-blowing or innovative. However, it's hands down one of the finest examples of a tastefully produced Hollywood blockbuster, one of those films that manage to meet the needs of all kinds of viewers.

I expected the whole movie to be centered on Vito Corleone, and was surprised to find Michael as the real protagonist. I didn't like him at first, but his captivating transformation from an honest war hero into a cold-blooded mafia boss makes is what made this film so captivating.

The production and cinematography are top-level: Coppola's subtle camerawork and the cast performances allow us to be naturally sucked in and get lost in the narration despite the demanding running time. The exotic atmosphere of post-war American Mafia is carefully recreated with an elegant touch, with unusually dark shots and shadows on the characters' faces to represent their duality. It's impossible not to notice how the shadows are taking on Michael's face as he gets more and more involved in the family business.

The ending has been praised as one of the most intense ever, but I actually thought it was a bit underwhelming. The way the executions are put in contrast with the baptism of Connie's child definitely has its impact, but I thought Michael had it a bit too easy there, especially if we think about how slow the buildup to Sollozzo's murder was. His marriage in Sicily felt a bit rushed as well, even though it served as one more way to show how different Michael is compared to the man of honor and family values that his father used to be.

"The Godfather": An Unparalleled Cinematic Masterpiece

Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather," released in 1972, stands as an enduring testament to the artistry of filmmaking. Adapted from Mario Puzo's novel of the same name, this crime saga has transcended its genre, becoming a cultural touchstone and setting the standard for cinematic excellence. With its compelling narrative, remarkable performances, and masterful direction, "The Godfather" has etched its place in the annals of cinema as an unparalleled masterpiece.

At its core, "The Godfather" is a gripping exploration of power, family, and the American Dream. The narrative follows the Corleones, a powerful Italian-American mafia family led by the patriarch Vito Corleone, portrayed with magnetic gravitas by Marlon Brando. The film opens with a wedding, a celebration that quickly morphs into a stage for the Corleones' complex web of relationships and the intricate power dynamics of the criminal underworld.

Brando's portrayal of Vito Corleone is nothing short of iconic. His raspy voice, measured cadence, and the subtle nuances in his performance elevate the character beyond the confines of a stereotypical mob boss. Brando's ability to convey vulnerability, authority, and a sense of morality makes Vito a multi-dimensional figure, rendering him unforgettable in the pantheon of cinema's greatest characters.

Equally commendable is Al Pacino's performance as Michael Corleone, Vito's initially reluctant son who is drawn into the family's criminal activities. Pacino's transformation from an outsider to a cold, calculating heir to the Corleone empire is a cinematic journey marked by subtle yet profound changes. It is a testament to Pacino's acting prowess that he navigates Michael's evolution with such authenticity and conviction.

Coppola's direction is a masterclass in storytelling. The pacing is deliberate, allowing the characters and the narrative to breathe. The film's cinematography, under the lens of Gordon Willis, is both evocative and atmospheric, capturing the grandeur of the Corleone estate and the grittiness of the criminal underworld. The iconic score, composed by Nino Rota, further enriches the viewing experience, creating an indelible emotional connection to the unfolding drama.

"The Godfather" is a narrative tapestry woven with intricate threads of power, loyalty, and betrayal. The screenplay, co-written by Coppola and Puzo, expertly balances the intimate moments within the family with the grand machinations of the crime syndicate. The dialogue is memorable, often quoted, and imbued with layers of meaning that invite contemplation on morality and the consequences of one's choices.

Beyond its narrative and performances, "The Godfather" endures for its profound impact on cinema as an art form. It set the template for future crime dramas, influencing a generation of filmmakers who sought to capture the same level of authenticity and complexity in their works. The film's cultural impact is undeniable, with references and homages permeating popular culture, cementing its status as a cinematic touchstone.

In conclusion, "The Godfather" is a cinematic tour de force that transcends its genre, standing as a crowning achievement in storytelling, acting, and direction. With its timeless themes and unforgettable characters, it remains a benchmark against which all other films in the crime genre are measured. More than four decades after its release, "The Godfather" continues to captivate audiences and reaffirm its status as a masterpiece in the pantheon of cinematic achievements.

The portrayal of mob life in the post-war era seemed realistic enough, and the appropriate atmosphere was set. The opening scenes (revolving around Don Corleone's daughter's wedding) gave me mixed feelings. Brando, of course, won (and refused to accept) the Oscar for Best Actor for his portrayal of Corleone, but I wasn't actually taken with his performance. It's not that I thought this was a bad movie. It was quite watchable and for the most part very interesting. I just think I've seen better.

8.title: My Big Fat Sicilian Wedding
8.content:
Big shout out to Flashback Cinemas for helping me finally, FINALLY, get this off my list of shame.

Of course now I'm left in the precarious position of having seen it and NOT thinking it's the best thing ever. I really wonder how much of that is due to the films own legendary status because it's impossible to go into this for the first time and not know it's supposed to be one of the finest pieces of cinema ever crafted.

I mean don't get me wrong, it's good. The performances are... WHAT HAPPENED TO AL PACINO?! I didn't know he could even do this! I think my first exposure to Pacino was The Devil's Advocate and he's been pretty over the top in most things I've seen but in this he's so quiet and understated but you know there's alot beneath the surface. Brando is great. Would have liked subtitles though for him, honestly.

I think what I most appreciated though was the way it handles the audience. These days it seems like most movies can't do anything without trying to explain everything. We get inundated with exposition but not here. Things are laid out beautifully so that just by paying attention you pick up on what's going on and who people are.

There are a LOT of people though. With a lot of very Italian names. Had a bit of trouble keeping the rooster straight in my head. Fortunately this is one I'd definitely enjoy revisiting, which I can only imagine to be a deeply rewarding experience because it feels like there are a lot of layers here to explore and new things to hone in on.

It's a great movie. I just don't think any movie could really live up to the massive hype machine of The Godfather. I can only imagine my estimation of it increasing though with future viewing.

8.title: Timeless Epic of Crime
8.content:
The dimmed lights pierced through the curtains, illuminating a room full of tense faces glued to the big screen. In the hushed room, muffled whispers and chuckles accompanied the haunting classical music. That night, I was immersed in the dark world of The Godfather, a film that has become an icon in the world of cinema.

From the beginning, Francis Ford Coppola managed to captivate the audience with his rich visuals and a chilling atmosphere. Every corner of the room, every glance, and every movement of the hand felt so meaningful. The dramatic lighting and stunning cinematography made the viewers feel the tension experienced by the characters.

Marlon Brando as Don Vito Corleone was extraordinary. His wrinkled face and raspy voice became a symbol of strength and wisdom. Every word that came out of his mouth felt weighty and meaningful. Brando successfully brought to life the figure of a father and leader who was full of charisma but also cruelty.

Al Pacino as young Michael Corleone was equally impressive. His transformation from a naive young man to a ruthless mafia boss was very convincing. His inner struggle between family love and the ambition of power became one of the most interesting core stories.

The Godfather is not just a film about crime. This film is a deep portrait of family, loyalty, and power. The Corleone family is depicted as a very strong unit, where blood ties and loyalty are very important values. However, behind that strength lies a terrifying dark side.

One of the most memorable scenes for me was Michael Corleone's baptism scene. This scene brought together two very different worlds: the religious world and the world of crime. In one scene, we see how Michael coldly plans a murder while taking a baptismal oath. This scene became a symbol of the complex duality of human beings.

The dialogues in this film are also very intelligent and meaningful. Every word uttered by the characters feels full of calculation and strategy. Coppola managed to create a world that was so realistic, where every decision had very big consequences.

However, The Godfather is not just about violence and political intrigue. This film also presents a tragic love story between Michael and Kay. Their love story became a kind of oasis in the desert of cruelty. However, in the end, love must lose to ambition and power.

After watching The Godfather, I felt shocked and tossed around by various emotions. This film made me ponder many things, from the meaning of family, the nature of power, to morality. The Godfather is a complex and nuanced film, so every viewer will find a different interpretation.

8.title: One of the best mafia movies

Few people do not know about the existence of this film. At least because of private mentions, references and parodies, almost everyone knows that there is such a film and about what it is about. However, if you read a brief description of the picture or do not watch the movie very carefully, you may get the impression that this is an ordinary film about bandits. So what makes this movie great? The answer is how it was filmed, staged and with what references to world culture.

Indeed, this simple, at first glance, movie about the path of one of the criminal families in the USA of the middle of the last century begins to play with completely new colors, if you carefully look behind the scenes, how it is staged by the director, what and why the actors say and what symbolism there is in all these scenes. And then, lo and behold, the cinema is transformed. In the way mafia boss don Carleone sits, you can see paintings by Caravaggio, the number of biblical references is difficult to count, and banal bandits for the first time at that time for cinema appear before the viewer as complex and dramatic characters, as if from the pen of Shakespeare.

8.title: Don't Take This Review Too Seriously
8.content:
Once upon a time, in the suburbs of the Big Apple, there was a man named Vito Corleone who made his fortune selling olive oil. The Corleone family's olive oil business was top-notch, thanks to a combination of quality products and a unique customer appreciation campaign that included complimentary silencers and silk ties. With such marketing genius, it's no wonder they became the envy of their rivals.

Then, a Turkish businessman wanted to get into the olive oil game in America. So, he asked Vito to invest in his operation. Fearing that Turkish olive oil was corrupting the youth, Vito turned him down. This refusal led to a feud, and in a botched assassination attempt at a fruit vendor, Vito miraculously survived. The family's fortunes took a nosedive, and the youngest son, Michael, skipped town to Italy to lay low and search for new olive oil sources. Meanwhile, the eldest son, Sonny, took over the family business but met a tragic end when he was gunned down at a toll plaza. After his brother's demise, Michael returned to the U. S. with a determination to stabilize olive oil prices once and for all...

The Godfather not only vividly portrays the fierce competition of the 1940s olive oil market; but also offers a treasure trove of life lessons that you'd find in a Chicken Soup for the Dark Soul book or a fortune cookie written by a mobster. Francis Ford Coppola's transformation of this olive oil odyssey into a trilogy of films, all bearing the same title yet each possessing its unique charm, is a cinematic rarity that exposes the absurdity of the industry. Coppola's direction, combined with the stellar performances, ensures that the misadventures of the Corleone family will captivate audiences for generations to come. After all, who knew olive oil could be the root of all evil, or so it seems?

Certainly! "The Godfather" (1972) is a cinematic masterpiece that stands the test of time as one of the greatest films ever made. Directed by Francis Ford Coppola and based on the novel by Mario Puzo, the film offers a deep dive into the complex world of the Corleone family, a New York mafia dynasty.

Marlon Brando delivers an iconic performance as Vito Corleone, the aging patriarch of the Corleone family, earning him an Academy Award for Best Actor. His portrayal of the Godfather is nuanced and powerful, with a presence that dominates the screen without the need for excessive dialogue or action.

Al Pacino shines as Michael Corleone, the youngest son who transforms from a reluctant outsider to the ruthless mafia boss. His character's arc is compelling and tragic, marking Pacino's rise as a formidable actor in Hollywood.

The film's narrative is rich and engaging, weaving a tale of family, honor, and betrayal. The storytelling is both intimate and grand, allowing viewers to sympathize with characters who are morally ambiguous yet deeply human. The cinematography and period detail immerse the audience in the era, while Nino Rota's haunting score underscores the emotional weight of the story.

"The Godfather" is not just about crime; it's a story about the American Dream seen through the lens of an immigrant family striving for power and respect in a new world. It's a reflection on loyalty, legacy, and the corrupting influence of absolute power.

In conclusion, "The Godfather" is a timeless epic that transcends its genre to become a profound exploration of the human condition. Its influence on cinema and culture is undeniable, and it remains a touchstone for filmmakers and moviegoers alike.

Marlon Brando delivers an iconic performance as Don Vito Corleone, the aging patriarch grappling with succession and a changing world.

Cinematography is masterful, with hauntingly beautiful shots that capture both the grandeur and intimacy of the Corleone world. Nino Rota's score is another standout, its melancholic themes underscoring the film's tragic inevitability.

The Godfather isn't afraid to confront the brutal realities of organized crime, but it also delves into complex themes of loyalty, honor, and family. Coppola masterfully blurs the lines between good and evil, forcing viewers to question their own moral compass.

The film's impact on cinema is undeniable. Its influence can be seen in countless subsequent gangster films and beyond. The Godfather is a timeless classic, a must-watch for anyone who appreciates exceptional filmmaking.

8.title: Honestly? It's a bit over-hyped

Now, I have to start by saying I just watched it for the first time ever, so I am definitely looking at it with fresh, modern eyes. And that being said, I just don't see it. Maybe it was this masterpiece in its time, but I don't actually think it holds that well in today's standards.

People seem to praise its directing and acting, but I don't really see how they are that special, to be honest. Goodfellas is definitely the better one at both of these. The directing and acting were good, yes, but a masterpiece? You can't even hear half of the words Marlon Brando speaks.

The strongest point was the interesting plot and it is great, even if it lacked a few good twists. The story arc overall is good and Al Pacino's character goes through a good development. On the other hand, the pacing could have been better and one or two times it felt maybe a bit boring even. The runtime could have easily been cut by 10-20 minutes or the boring acts could have been improved.

In general, I kind of didn't like how they romanticized the whole mobster life. And this is indeed why I prefer Goodfellas over this: that movie showed what kind of maniacs and psychopaths criminals and gangster must be to survive in that underground world. This made it look like anyone could have changed their career to become a criminal.

Anyhow, it absolutely is worth a watch and it's one of the most important parts of cinema history and I am embarrassed to admit it took me all these years to watch. But I finally. And if you like well acted and well directed gangster/mobster/crime cinema, I would definitely suggest to also turn to Breaking Bad and Peaky Blinders (even though they are not movies, but series, they are the modern day masterpieces of directing and acting).

8.title: A Timeless Masterpiece: The Godfather Drama
8.content:
Few films have managed to captivate audiences for generations, and Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather" is undeniably one of them. Released in 1972, this crime drama stands as a timeless masterpiece that continues to resonate with viewers, transcending time and leaving an indelible mark on cinema history.

Set in the turbulent world of organized crime, "The Godfather" is a rich tapestry of power, loyalty, family, and the moral dilemmas that accompany a life steeped in violence. The film introduces us to the Corleones, an Italian-American mafia family led by the enigmatic Don Vito Corleone (portrayed flawlessly by Marlon Brando). Brando's portrayal is nothing short of iconic, showcasing his exceptional acting prowess and cementing his place as one of the greatest actors of all time.

The storytelling in "The Godfather" is masterful, thanks to the impeccable screenplay by Coppola and Mario Puzo, who adapted his own novel for the screen. Every scene is meticulously crafted, drawing the audience into the intricacies of the Corleone family's world. The film strikes a perfect balance between character development and the relentless progression of its narrative, keeping viewers on the edge of their seats from beginning to end.

What sets "The Godfather" apart from other crime dramas is its attention to detail and its exploration of complex themes. It delves into the dynamics of power and the consequences of choosing a life governed by ruthless ambition. The moral ambiguity of the characters forces us to question our own values and judgments, blurring the line between good and evil. It's a testament to the film's brilliance that we find ourselves sympathizing with characters whose actions we would typically condemn.

Beyond its engaging story and unforgettable characters, "The Godfather" boasts stunning cinematography that enhances the atmosphere of each scene. The film's visual aesthetic, coupled with its meticulously crafted sets and costumes, transports us to a bygone era, immersing us in the world of 1940s New York. The haunting musical score, composed by Nino Rota, further heightens the tension and emotion, serving as a perfect complement to the unfolding drama.

The performances in "The Godfather" are uniformly exceptional. Al Pacino shines as Michael Corleone, Don Vito's reluctant son who undergoes a profound transformation throughout the film. Pacino's portrayal of a man torn between loyalty and self-preservation is a masterclass in acting, and his performance paved the way for a long and illustrious career.

In summary, "The Godfather" is an unparalleled cinematic achievement that continues to captivate audiences. Its enduring legacy lies not only in its brilliant storytelling, exceptional performances, and technical prowess but also in its exploration of timeless themes that resonate with viewers across generations. This crime drama stands tall as a testament to the power of cinema and its ability to transport us into the lives of complex characters and morally ambiguous worlds. If you haven't experienced "The Godfather" yet, do yourself a favor and immerse yourself in this cinematic masterpiece that remains as compelling today as it was over four decades ago.

8.title: agreed
8.content:
"Marlon Brando is Don Vito Corleone, head of perhaps the most powerful New York-area mafia family in the 1940s, in this well-respected film by director/writer Francis Ford Coppola. As the film begins, Vito is receiving "business" guests in his office at his home while his daughter Connie's (Talia Shire) wedding and reception are taking place. The epic plot takes place over many years, telling the story of Vito, his family--including Michael (Al Pacino), Santino (James Caan) and Tom Hagen (Robert Duvall), his associates, and their interactions with other mob syndicates.

The Godfather is commonly considered to be one of the "greatest films of all time". Even though I've given it a 10, I wouldn't put that same kind of exalted emphasis on it. I've given literally thousands of films 10s over the years, and for me, Godfather just barely made a 10. I think it has a number of flaws, but Coppola also has a knack for transcending the problems with some brilliant move or another. At any rate, it is definitely must-see viewing--even if it's only because it's so highly regarded--if you've not experienced the film yet. I think it's a good idea to attain cultural literacy, and films as popularly loved as The Godfather become necessary elements in achieving that literacy.

Shorn of its gangster trappings, The Godfather is sprawling and soap-operatic in tone. The sprawl is appropriate to its origins as a novel by Mario Puzo, who also co-wrote the screenplay with Coppola. There is a large cast of characters--maybe too large, as it can be difficult to keep track of just who everyone is. Even after you've watched the film a couple times you may find scenes where mobsters seem to spontaneously appear and you catch yourself saying, "Wait, who is that guy supposed to be again?" The soap opera angle can be a positive or negative depending on your tastes. I tend to not like soap-operatic stories, but of course Coppola put yummy gangster topping on this one to make it palatable for guys like me. At root, though, The Godfather is concerned with realistic depictions of a very dysfunctional family as they try to make it through life--including marriages, births, adultery, spats between family members, tiffs with others in their community, and so on. My theory is that the soap opera angle accounts for much of the film's appeal. For me, it (and the slight lack of focus from the sprawl) accounts for much of the reason that I barely gave the film a 10.

But two things help the film transcend a lower score for me. Even though the gangster stuff has been far surpassed in graphic brutality in the intervening years, the dramatic context of the violence usually gives it tremendous impact. Films like Ichi the Killer (2001), which I just watched for the first time the night before watching The Godfather again, make the Godfather's brutality fit for Sesame Street in comparison. However, although Ichi's violence is effective, setting that knob to "11" doesn't make it better. Besides, Ichi is so over the top that it would make many Godfather fans want to hurl.

To the extent that Coppola and Puzo just focus on the extended Corleone family, they create tremendous depth in their relationships. The whole film can be looked at as a fascinating depiction of "oscillating" dynamics in the family, with the pole pairs being interacting/distancing, control/lack of control, benevolence/malevolence. Most character stances and actions are some combination of those ranges of characteristics, and everyone dances around the poles, so to speak, throughout the film. From this angle, even the attractive surface violence (well, attractive to us fans of that stuff in artworks) is mainly there for the purpose of pushing characters more to one pole or the other. There is an implication that underlying these mechanisms is some natural tendency towards achieving (a dynamic) equilibrium.

But there are more superficial stylistic factors that help push my score up to a 10, also. The most obvious, which everyone and their grandparents have mentioned, are the performances. It's tough to go wrong when you have a cast including Al Pacino, Marlon Brando, Robert Duvall, James Caan, Diane Keaton, and so on. Another commonly mentioned element that I agree is fantastic and superbly integrated to create atmosphere is Nino Rota's score.

Less often mentioned is the consistently intriguing cinematography by Gordon Willis. Most of Willis' unusual shots in the film are so subtle as to be barely noticeable unless you're looking for them. The opening, for example, consists of a long (it lasts a few minutes) "zoom out" from Amerigo Bonasera (Salvatore Corsitto). The shot is beautifully lit--most of the frame is extremely dark, giving Bonasera a chiaroscuro effect (the opening is also unusual in that it's a long monologue from a minor character).

Willis and Coppola have a knack for placing their actors in the frame to create depth and interesting visual patterns. This is done so slyly that at first blush you wouldn't believe it's something they thought about, but if you keep this in mind while watching, you can see delightful visual paths that zigzag, wind to a focal point, and so on, all created by the confluence of actors and scenery in the frame.

If you haven't seen The Godfather before, the most important thing you can do before watching is to forget about all of the "greatest film of all time" hype. That's only likely to set up expectations that could never be met; more than likely you'll be disappointed. Just think of it as one of the better films from one of Hollywood's more admirable but relatively odder directors, featuring earlier performances from a very well known cast, and keep in mind that it's as much a "historical family saga" as a crime or gangster film. " I completely agree

8.title: Classic
8.content:
Epic in scope while maintaining a patience and intimacy characteristic of European art cinema, THE GODFATHER is rightly considered one of the greatest films ever made. The Godfather continues to influence producers of films, television shows, and video games more than 30 years after its release. Nino Rota's score, the sumptuous set design, and Brando's raspy pseudo-whisper have become part of our collective cultural memory.

The film possesses an operatic quality, yet it's more understated than it is flamboyant. It takes its subjects seriously, bestowing legitimacy upon the internecine power struggles of the Mafia normally reserved for classical themes in high art. The film's release initiated a period when American filmmakers dared to take themselves and their artistic ambitions seriously (perhaps too seriously). There is something deeply resonant in the film's treatment of filial piety, the need for respect, and our culture's abiding interest in the parallel moral universe of the Mafia.

8.title: The Godfather is in no short supply of action and suspense.
8.content:
The Godfather

Smart. That's how I describe `The Godfather'. Every aspect of this film is dripping with intellect. The directing, the writing, the cinematography, and the acting. And all the elements of the film are woven tightly together to make a very entertaining package. The intricate plot follows the development of Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) and the enthralling drama that pursues his `family'. The script does the impossible task of capturing the complex politics of organized crime, and makes it interesting to boot. The plot leads the audience along its windy path where it comes across many peaks until it finally builds to the fantastic finale. To achieve this famous finish, the director employs the use of some pretty clever technical tricks. To achieve suspense, he cleverly places the camera at angles that leads the audience one way, until he surprises them with the real result later on. He also infuses the sound of the church organ music and the crying baby, and then gradually increases the decibels subtly and effectively. That technique pulled the viewers in and made their knuckles white during the climax of the film. The director was skillful in his mastery of all the film's techniques and in getting what he needed from the actors. This strong cast of cast of actors included Marlon Brando, Al Pacino, Robert Duvall, and James Conn. Each actor portrayed their characters profoundly. Marlon Brando executed method acting techniques in a way that only a veteran like Marlon could. Al Pacino clearly shows his character (Michael Corleone) grow and change. His acting is subtle, confident and quiet until it explodes in an awesome rage. Michael Corleone is much like the entire movie. `The Godfather' is subtle and complex, and it builds to the memorable finish. `The Godfather' stimulates the mind and starts the blood and adrenaline pumping in anyone who watches it. That is why I recommend this beautiful masterpiece to anyone and everyone with a thirst for quality film.

8.title: The Godfather(1972) IS THE BEST FATHER !!
8.content:
This is a masterpiece. A timeless masterpiece. Initially, I didn't like this film all that much - I found it rather over-hyped and boring. This was until the advent of DVD, which gave me the feature I needed for this sort of film: subtitles. Once I switched them on and heard (read) every last word of Brando's ramblings and other characters ramblings, I grew a true appreciation for this epic.

To make a true epic, you need all of three following ingredients working in near perfect harmony. For screenwriters who come across this, take the following pointers on board: 1) Contrasting Characters: Good films have some character distinction, but most fall rather flat because the core of each character is the same.

Of course, there are exceptions to rule (ie... where you want mono-tonal characters... aka matrix; or where you want outlandish contrasts... aka The Fifth Element), but ultimately, this is what makes films deep, meaningful and grand. Consider the contrasts between the Don's children. Michael is rather cool, rational and collected, whereas Sonny is more hot-headed, spontaneous and simple minded. But simply having these contrasts is not nearly enough. What you really need to do is to develop these characters - place them in situations - and then dwell on how their character impacts on the situation they're put in. The Godfather is a terrific example of how to pull this off. While many try to do this in screenplays, most lose the plot and create character obscurities that stretch credibility.

2) Transformation: The central character(s) must undergo a transformation, resulting in them being almost unrecognizable by the end of the film. By putting them into situations, the character's character must not only influence the outcome of the situation; it must also have a lasting impact on the character. Consider Michael at the wedding and compare that to the Michael we see at the end of the film. Again, many films try, but most fail because they come up with unreal (literally, not praisingly) or simply moronic transformations (eg, Wall Street).

3) Patience: Men in Black 2 was an astounding film for one simple reason - it was an entire film squashed into about 70 minutes. It was not much longer than an episode of ER or Buffy. I certainly hope the new goal of Hollywood isn't to make films as short as possible.

All the great ones spend time - time developing characters, family life, growth, patience with the story telling in general. This is the key (provided that the story isn't mind-numbingly boring). Dances with Wolves, Heat.. and so on are very patient but top-class films. While studios may be lukewarm on the idea of longer films, they are worth it if you have a ripper story to base it on.

Don Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando) is the head of a mafia family living in New York. The Don's main source of income is gambling and protection. Another head of another mafia family (Sollozzo) wants to sell drugs to gain profit, Don Vito hates the idea of selling drugs on the market, so an attempt to take his life is made. One special son of the Godfather is brought to light when this event happens. In the film directed by Francis Ford Coppola, the films gives the viewer a feeling of sympathy for a mob family, when in reality, a person does not usually take the side of a mob family, doing things against the law to make profit. A couple of the ways this happens is the fact that it's felt that Don Corleone is trying to do the `right' and `honest' way to make his profit by not selling drugs. Also, by the death and injury of many family members, the film brings a feeling of understanding, sympathy, and compassion towards the Corleone's. The film includes numerous scenes of murder, often in an offensive amount. Some scene feature hideous lights jobs, to the point of not seeing the character's faces, or telling what is happening. Although very monotonous, the music and soundtrack the movie was well done, and really changed the feel of individual scenes. There was an excellent job of doing crescendos and making diminuendos of certain scene to build suspense, or foreshadowing an event. Overall, the acting was superb, great casting, very well conceived and structured plot. I give The Godfather 8.5 out of ten.

THE GODFATHER is quite simply a masterful piece of film-making, an epic in the truest sense of the word and by far the finest gangster film ever shot. Made with finesse, style to spare and a director who elicits pitch-perfect performances from a talented cast, this is movie-making as it should be.

8.title: Best movie
8.content:
Francis Ford Coppola's The Godfather is more than just a film-it is a cinematic masterpiece that has stood the test of time. Based on Mario Puzo's novel, the movie explores themes of power, loyalty, and family in the world of organized crime.

At the heart of the story is the Corleone family, led by the aging patriarch Vito Corleone (Marlon Brando in an iconic performance). His reluctant son, Michael (Al Pacino), undergoes a compelling transformation from a war hero uninterested in the family business to a ruthless mafia leader. This character arc is one of the most fascinating in film history, brilliantly portrayed by Pacino.

The film is a masterclass in storytelling, cinematography, and character development. Coppola's direction, combined with Nino Rota's haunting score and Gordon Willis' moody cinematography, creates an immersive experience. Every scene is meticulously crafted, from the chilling opening sequence to the gripping finale.

What makes The Godfather exceptional is its balance between crime drama and a deeply personal family saga. The film humanizes its characters while never glorifying their violent world. With standout performances, memorable dialogue, and a powerful narrative, The Godfather remains one of the greatest films ever made.

Seriously, though, this stellar 4K offering will doubtless remain one of the best - if not the best - home market releases of the year. The films themselves need no introduction. The Godfather (1972) immediately emerged as a cultural milestone; The Godfather Part II (1974) is lauded in some corners (although not this one) as being superior to its predecessor; and The Godfather Part III (1990), refashioned here as Coppola's definitive The Godfather Coda: The Death of Michael Corleone, is worthwhile yet seriously flawed (go here for a full review). The first two films earned Best Picture Academy Awards, with the original also winning for Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Actor for Marlon Brando; the icon delivers a cheeky (in more ways than one) performance as Don Vito Corleone, although the award clearly should have gone to the real star, Al Pacino (relegated to the Best Supporting Actor category, where he competed against co-stars James Caan and Robert Duvall). Part II earned a total of six statues, including Best Director and Best Supporting Actor for Robert De Niro as the young Don Vito Corleone.

8.title: 8.1/10 - A Tragedy, Soaked with Shadows
8.content:
I'm super close to finishing the IMDb top 100 poster now, and I'm so, so hyped for that. It's been three and a half years since I've started, and getting so close to the top is unreal. Now, in my journey throughout this poster, I've came across all sorts of movies, expectations-wise: movies that I've heard little to nothing about beforehand, movies that have already been on my watchlist when I got the poster, movies I've seen but many years back, movies that are only there because people from a specific country love them (I'm looking at you, India). The thing I'm getting at is this: my expectations from movies are varied and very individual to each movie, and they are influenced by a lot of things. The Godfather is one of the movies I've been hearing about for years now, knowing how immensely impactful it is on cinema. Friends, fellow film lovers, one of my sisters - everyone just kept telling me I HAVE to watch it, a feeling that has only gotten stronger after watching Apocalypse Now - a great war movie by the same director - but me going from bottom to top on this poster meant not getting to watch this one for years, and I knew that when I started this whole journey. Now I'm here, though, after my rewatch to this film. Let's get into it.

The Godfather is a 1972 film by Francis Ford Coppola, based on Mario Puzo's book by the same name. The movie follows the Corleone family, an Italian mafia family in 1940's New York. The movie tells their story throughout a decade or so, with special focus on Michael Corleone (Al Pacino), the least involved in the family business of all the men of the family, and the way he gets pulled into the conflict - and the family business - when things go awry, and a bloody war starts with another big mafia family.

The first thing to catch my attention here is the cinematography. Many a film nerd have talked about how each shot here is soaked with shadows, and how the inner mafia world contrasts with the innocent, well-lit exterior in scenes like the famous wedding in the first act. They have crowned the cinematographer, Gordon Willis, as "prince of darkness", and analyzed each scene down to the last frame. Honestly, though? This is just, simply put, one the best-looking movie I've watched in quite a while, easily. It's not just the lighting - it's the composition, the attention to the background, the color grading. I think about a beautifully shot scene at a funeral, with flowers in the background, I recall another in a little garden where oranges grow, and so many more pop to mind. Even supposedly simple shots, with just one or two characters and very simplistic background, can become hellish, desperate, soaked in grief of sorts. The movie really does a great job on that front.

The dialogue is very iconic, too, with many lines popping up when looking back at the movie. It's not just about being quotable, referenced endlessly and everywhere - it's about the film's ability to make dramatic impact. When looking at today's mainstream cinema (and cinema in general, throughout history, though I do feel like in recent years it's been more of a phenomenon), so many movies are trying to pull off badass moments of dialogue, to be cool, to ingrain a moment into our brains, but when they have nothing up their sleeve it just makes everything cringy, tryhard, stiff (side note: you're more than welcome to read my latest film review, for The Dark Knight Rises, an example to such a movie). The Godfather manages to pull off so many great lines of dialogue with a lot of dramatic impact, and almost effortlessly at that - much of that thanks to actors such as Al Pacino and Marlon Brando, who deliver very good, natural performances here. Showing these underworld interactions in a movie and making it believable, well-written enough to not break the immersion - well, that takes some skill, and the people who were working on this movie definitely had it, and it shows.

In movies, and generally media, of this sort - you know, crime-centered stories that depict characters who get sucked into the underworld - the world of crime often seems alluring, luxurious, brimming with wealth. Even safer than the "ordinary" world, at times. But sooner or later it is revealed, in many of these stories, that the characters have been dancing on thin, thin ice for this whole time, and their bloody dance can make them fall right into cold, hellish depths just like that, swallowed by their greed and the violence of the underworld. The way that even in their happiest days they need to look over their shoulder, the tension between this deep, familial, loving bonds, that mix in the so-called "business" so much that it's hard to understand if the family is the goal and the crime is the means, or if it's vice versa - there's something very tragic about it all. I think that the movie captures this very well. We care for the characters, and when they fall into the dark pits of the underworld it has an impact, especially when we know that things could've been so much simpler had they chosen another path. And besides, just the tragedy of being born into it, being connected to evil acts by blood, knowing you could never escape your name, creates this dark feeling of determinism, dark fate. Works well.

Pretty much every male character here behaves like douchebags at least in some instances - violence, self-importance, misogyny, you know the drill. It's easy to notice that these characters act in ways that are not only illegal, but are also often immoral, or at least morally problematic. Despite that, we also get to see their more caring side, the bonds they have with each other, the love and respect they have for Vito. I feel like we're shown different facets in ways that really make the main characters feel more human, even though they're knee-deep in the crime world. And kudos to the actors, again, for delivering characters with complexities in a convincing, immersive way, especially Brando as Vito, who steals the focus of the plot even when he's off-screen. My point being: the characters here are written in a way that reveals both their humanity and their darker sides, which makes us relate to them just enough to be emotionally invested, and emphasizes the tension between those two sides. I like the movie's approach to that.

The pacing is also solid, which is not to be taken for granted - pacing can be a challenging thing to manage with movies of this sort, that let their plot unfold throughout a decade or so, and a pretty long runtime, too. With The Godfather there's almost always something interesting going on, some tension, this pulling sensation that makes me want to discover more. I wouldn't say that this movie has kept me at the edge of my seat constantly, but I would say that the pacing here is indeed solid, especially in the final act. This movie is a bit of a slow burn, in some ways, but it's always in escalation, always raising the stakes and making the characters change. I will also say here that the soundtrack is very solid as well - it just works well when it comes to creating an atmosphere, and it's used pretty well. It's not my favorite soundtrack ever by any means, but it's recognizable, echoing the tragic themes this movie is focusing on, and it usually hits the spot.

The Godfather is a tragic portrayal of a crime family who's getting sucked into a bloody war, where no one can stay uninvolved, no family member can step aside and let everything drift away. It's the best-looking film I've seen in quite a while, and it shows characters from every angle, the loving and caring one as well as the harsh, violent, ruthless one. A rise and a fall, a fall and a rise - no stability can be expected when living on the thin ice. The tension between business and family here, and the alluring luxury of the underworld, made me think of Breaking Bad, which, though maybe anachronistic, is a big compliment when it comes from me. I'm feeling an 8.1/10 on this one. A very good movie indeed.

8.title: Great movie
8.content:
"The first time I watched The Godfather, I was a teenager, and honestly, I didn't appreciate it as much as I should have. At the time, I found the pacing too slow and didn't fully grasp the depth of the story or its significance. I dismissed it as something that wasn't for me and moved on.

However, after revisiting the film 20 years later, I decided to give it another chance, and I have to admit, I was completely wrong in my initial judgment. Watching it now with more life experience, I can truly appreciate the brilliance of the storytelling, the deliberate pacing, and the intricate character development. Every scene serves a purpose, and what once seemed slow to me now feels like a masterpiece of tension, emotion, and complexity.

The Godfather is not just a movie, but a profound exploration of power, loyalty, and family. I'm glad I gave it a second chance because it has become one of my favorite films, and I finally understand why it's considered one of the greatest of all time."

8.title: A great movie
8.content:
This is a masterpiece. A timeless masterpiece. Initially, I didn't like this film all that much - I found it rather over-hyped and boring. This was until the advent of DVD, which gave me the feature I needed for this sort of film: subtitles. Once I switched them on and heard (read) every last word of Brando's ramblings and other characters ramblings, I grew a true appreciation for this epic.

To make a true epic, you need all of three following ingredients working in near perfect harmony. For screenwriters who come across this, take the following pointers on board: 1) Contrasting Characters: Good films have some character distinction, but most fall rather flat because the core of each character is the same.

Of course, there are exceptions to rule (ie... where you want mono-tonal characters... aka matrix; or where you want outlandish contrasts... aka The Fifth Element), but ultimately, this is what makes films deep, meaningful and grand. Consider the contrasts between the Don's children. Michael is rather cool, rational and collected, whereas Sonny is more hot-headed, spontaneous and simple minded. But simply having these contrasts is not nearly enough. What you really need to do is to develop these characters - place them in situations - and then dwell on how their character impacts on the situation they're put in. The Godfather is a terrific example of how to pull this off. While many try to do this in screenplays, most lose the plot and create character obscurities that stretch credibility.

8.title: The Godfather: A Masterpiece of Cinema
8.content:
Francis Ford Coppola's "The Godfather," based on Mario Puzo's novel, is a cinematic tour de force that continues to captivate audiences decades after its release. This 1972 film, starring Marlon Brando as the patriarch Vito Corleone and Al Pacino as his son Michael, delves deep into the complexities of power, loyalty, and family within the Mafia world.

From the opening scene, the film immerses viewers in a rich, atmospheric narrative. Brando's portrayal of Vito Corleone is iconic, exuding a quiet but formidable presence. Pacino's transformation from the reluctant war hero to the ruthless head of the family is nothing short of mesmerizing. The supporting cast, including James Caan, Robert Duvall, and Diane Keaton, deliver exceptional performances that enhance the film's depth.

Coppola's direction, coupled with Nino Rota's haunting score, creates a timeless atmosphere. The cinematography, with its meticulous attention to detail, brings 1940s New York to life. The film's pacing allows for a deep exploration of its characters, making their journey both compelling and believable.

"The Godfather" is more than a crime drama; it's a profound exploration of power and its consequences. Its legacy as one of the greatest films ever made is well-deserved, making it a must-watch for any cinema enthusiast.

8.content: This isn't just a beautifully crafted gangster film. Or an outstanding family portrait, for that matter. An amazing period piece. A character study. A lesson in filmmaking and an inspiration to generations of actors, directors, screenwriters and producers. For me, this is more: this is the definitive film.
